aOR I: Ocean Researcher I; OR II: Ocean Researcher II. bSailing along the KEEPKEY transect. ![Map of the study area and locations of sampling stations](page_1012_1342_670_377.png) Fig. 1. Map of the study area and locations of sampling stations. Filled circles (●) indicate KEEPKEY stations with the odd-numbered stations labeled. Stations off the KEEPKEY transect were visited during the April 1995 (○), the January 1996 (▲), and the April 1996 cruises (△), respectively. Names of the four hydrographic zones used in the text are marked above the corresponding stations. (Table 1). All cruise tracks ran in a cross-shelf direction and were approximately normal to isobaths (Fig. 1). Among them, eight cruises sailed along a transect starting at 26°20′N, 120°30′E and ending at 25°0′N, 123°10′E, and the other four cruises visited stations in the close vicinity. The major transect was named KEEPKEY transect since it has been frequently surveyed during the operation period of the KEEP (Kuroshio Edge Exchange Processes) project. The hydrography along the KEEPKEY transect is fairly well known and several zones can be recognized according to physical and chemical properties of sea water (Gong et al., 1995, 1996). The region between KEEPKEY stations 1 and 3 is the coastal zone, and is typically occupied by the low temperature, low salinity coastal water. Stations 5 and 7 belong to the mid-shelf zone occupied by low nutrient Taiwan Strait water, and stations 9 to 11 are usually occupied by high nutrient water from an upwelling system. The region between stations 15 and 17 is the Kuroshio zone. The euphotic zone in this region is always occupied by warm, nutrient-poor Kuroshio water (Fig. 1). Water samples for Trichodesmium enumeration were collected with a rosette sampler equipped with 2.5 l Go-Flo bottles (General Oceanics, Miami). One liter of sea water was transferred to plastic bottles and fixed immediately with acidic Lugol’s solution (Thronsdon, 1978). In the laboratory, phytoplankton cells in water samples were allowed to settle for at least 48 h and the supernatant was carefully withdrawn by an aspirator until about 50 ml remained in the bottle. The concentrated water sample was then transferred to a conical centrifuge tube and stored in dark at 4°C. Immediately before microscope examination, the sample was concentrated again to a final volume of 1 ml, and loaded to a Sedgwick–Rafter counting cell. The entire counting cell was scanned using a Nikon Optiphot-2 microscope at 100×, and number of trichomes (Trichodesmium filaments) encountered were used to evaluate Trichodesmium abundance. A small fraction of trichomes in our sample were less than 200 μm in length. These short trichomes were excluded in our counts to avoid bias. According to our preliminary experiment (Chang, 1999), Trichodesmium abundance generated this way showed no significant difference from filtering 1 l of sea water onto a Nuclepore filter on deck followed by epi-fluorescent microscope counting. Counting 10 samples repeatedly collected from the same depth at a station revealed that a single-sample estimate should carry a coefficient of variation of 62%. As a result, the present counting method was intended for the detection of abundance differences greater than an order of magnitude. A somewhat different method was adopted to count trichomes in samples from the July cruise in 1994. Samples were settled in 100 ml Utermöhl sedimentation cylinders and counted on a Nikon inverted-microscope (Hasle, 1978). Samples from the KEEPKEY station 1 of the May 1994 cruise have been counted by the Sedgwick–Rafter method and the Utermöhl method, and both methods did not detect any trichomes in the water column. An examination of the abundance of a chain-forming diatom, Rhizosolenia, in the same batch of samples revealed that the difference between these two counting methods ranged from 0 to 200%. Temperature and salinity data were measured with a Seabird CTD (SBE9/11 plus, Seabird Inc. WA). The mixed layer depth was obtained from the upper region on a density profile where the variation in \( \sigma_0 \) was less than 0.16. Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations were measured in duplicates using a Turner Designs Fluorometer (Model 10-AU-005) according to standard procedures (Parsons et al., 1984). Samples for nutrient determination were quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen and then stored at \( -18^\circ \mathrm{C} \) until analysis. The concentration of nitrate and nitrite were determined by the pink azo dye method, and phosphate were determined by the molybdenum blue method (Parsons et al., 1984; Pai et al., 1990; Gong, 1992). 3. Results In all samples, Trichodesmium mainly appeared as individual trichomes. Colonial forms existed, but were very rare. As a result, attempts were not made to distinguish between various species in this genus. Of all stations visited, Trichodesmium trichomes always existed in the surface layer (Figs. 2(a) and 3(a)). Population densities decreased rapidly when depth became greater than 50 m. A maximum of biomass usually occurred at a depth of 20–30 m. Sometimes, a second maximum appeared near sea surface (Fig. 3(a)). In the Kuroshio, the highest abundance occurred in May 1995, reaching 276 trichomes l\(^{-1}\) at KEEPKEY station 17 (Fig. 2(a)). The abundance was greatly reduced in winter months. At most a few trichomes were found in a liter of sea water. The depth-integrated Trichodesmium abundance showed a clear seasonal cycle with March to May as the growth phase and September to November as the decline phase (Fig. 2(b)). However, the year-to-year variation in Trichodesmium standing crop can not be overlooked. For example, in May 1995, \(10^7\) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) was observed in Kuroshio. In contrast, only \(10^5\) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) was observed at the end of April 1996, a reduction of 100 times (Fig. 2(b)). Environmental factors in Kuroshio possessed a similar seasonal cycle. Water temperature was 24\(^\circ\)C in winter, but increased to 29\(^\circ\)C in summer (Fig. 2(c)). As for mixing strength, strong northeast monsoons in winter generated a mixed layer more than 100 m thick. When weather became more stable in summer, the mixed layer depths were typically around 30 m. The seasonal variation of Trichodesmium standing crop in the upwelling region had a pattern resembling that in the Kuroshio with higher abundance in summer (Fig. 3(b)). The highest population density observed was 600 trichomes l\(^{-1}\). Compared to the seasonal cycle in the Kuroshio, Trichodesmium declined earlier in the upwelling region. Starting from the end of September, no trichomes were detected in this area. The cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium revealed different patterns in spring, summer, and fall. In spring, cold water with temperature around 20\(^\circ\)C occupied the area between the coast and the upwelling while Kuroshio water was still warmer than 24\(^\circ\)C (Fig. 4(a)). On the four cruises that covered the KEEPKEY transect in spring months, Trichodesmium was always undetectable in the coastal zone (Fig. 5(a)). However, at a distance of 150–250 km from shore, trichomes started to appear, and population densities increased toward Kuroshio. In contrast, phytoplankton biomass, as indicated by chlorophyll \(a\) concentrations, was constantly low in the Kuroshio (Fig. 4(d)). High levels of chlorophyll were usually observed at the outer fringe of the upwelling, apparently supported by the nutrients supplied from the deep (Figs. 4(b) and (c)). In fall, the difference in temperature between Kuroshio and coastal water was less than 3\(^\circ\) (Fig. 4(a)). A sudden drop near stations 11 to 13 marked the presence of cold Fig. 2. Trichodesmium vertical distribution and seasonal variation in the Kuroshio zone. (a) Representative abundance profiles observed in various seasons. (b) Seasonal variation of depth integrated abundance. The depth of integration was 50 m for KEEPKEY stations 1 to 5, and 70 m for stations 6 to 17, respectively. Various symbols are used to distinguish data collected from 1993 (○), 1994 (●), 1995 (▽), and 1996 (▼). The symbol marked by an arrow indicates that the actual value of that data point was 0 trichome m^{-2}. (c) Seasonal variation of temperature (■) and mixing depth (□) in Kuroshio. Water temperature were measured at 10 m depth. Curves are polynomial regression lines to indicate the general trend. water in the upwelling, and coincided with high concentrations of nutrients (Figs. 4(b) and (c)). Compared to the distribution of Trichodesmium in spring, a completely reversed pattern appeared in fall. Based on available data from two cruises in 1993 and 1995, Trichodesmium standing crop reached 1.6–3.2 \times 10^6 trichomes m^{-2} in the Fig. 3. Trichodesmium vertical distribution and seasonal variation in the upwelling zone. (a) Representative abundance profiles observed in various seasons. (b) Seasonal variation of depth integrated abundance. Symbols are the same as in Fig. 2(b), and the curve is a polynomial regression line to indicate the general trend. coastal zone but was virtually undetectable in the upwelling zone and Kuroshio (Fig. 5(b)). Relatively few data sets were obtained in summer. In July of 1994, a segment of the KEEPKEY transect on the outer shelf was surveyed, and water temperature was constantly warmer than 28°C (Fig. 4(a)). Trichodesmium abundance ranged from \( 5.7 \times 10^6 \) to \( 1.3 \times 10^7 \) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) with a mean trichome length of 107 cells. Substantial variation was observed between stations which indicated a patchy distribution (Fig. 5(b)). Such high abundance apparently did not occur in every summer. When KEEPKEY station 8 was visited in July 1995, the integrated abundance of Trichodesmium was merely \( 2.7 \times 10^4 \) trichomes m\(^{-2}\). 4. Discussion Our results indicated that the cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium changed annually with seasons (Fig. 5). The spring-type distribution with higher abundance in Fig. 4. Typical cross-shelf variation in seawater properties observed in spring (△, April 1996 cruise), summer (○, July 1994 cruise), and fall (●, October 1995 cruise). (a) Temperature measured at 10 m depth. (b) Depth integrated nitrate and nitrite concentration. The integration depth is the same as in Fig. 2. (c) Depth integrated phosphate concentration. (d) Phytoplankton standing stock expressed as chlorophyll \( a \) concentration. Kuroshio agreed well with patterns previously observed in the East China Sea (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974). The fall-type distribution with higher abundance in the coastal zone received less attention before, but other independent observations supported the existence of such a pattern. A survey in Taiwan Strait indicated that Trichodesmium reached annual maximum in September with the highest abundance at \( 2 \times 10^3 \) trichomes l\(^{-1}\) found near the mainland coast (Fujian Institute of Oceanology, (a) Spring ![Cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium in spring](page_370_312_670_370.png) (b) Summer (○) and Fall (△ ●) ![Cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium in summer and fall](page_370_740_670_670.png) Fig. 5. The cross-shelf distributions of Trichodesmium abundance observed in (a) spring and (b) summer and fall. The cruises were conducted in May 1994 (◇), March 1995 (▼), April 1995 (◆), April 1996 (▽), July 1994 (○), November 1993 (△), and October 1995 (●). 1988). In addition, all Trichodesmium blooms reported were very close to coast, and all occurred in summer and fall (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974; Hong et al., 1992). Temperature has long been recognized as a major factor that controls Trichodesmium abundance, and 20°C was considered as the minimum temperature for Trichodesmium to survive (Marumo and Nagasawa, 1976; Carpenter, 1983a). In spring, the scarcity of Trichodesmium in the coastal zone was apparently a result of poor growth due to the less than 20°C temperature (Figs. 4 and 5). As the temperature (a) Spring ![Scatter plot showing log (abundance+1) vs Temperature (°C) for spring distribution](page_324_312_1012_384.png) (b) Fall ![Scatter plot showing log (abundance+1) vs Temperature (°C) for fall distribution](page_324_748_1012_384.png) Fig. 6. The cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium explained by the variation in water temperature. (a) Spring distribution and temperature. Symbols are the same as in Fig. 5, and temperature was measured at 10 m depth. The straight line marks a significant regression relationship: \( \log (A + 1) = -0.401 + 0.252\ T \) (\( P < 0.05, r = 0.56 \)), where \( A \) is the integrated Trichodesmium abundance (trichomes m\(^{-2}\)), and \( T \) is temperature. All non-zero data from the four spring cruises were included in the regression. (b) Fall distribution and temperature. The regression generated nonsignificant result. Symbols are the same as in Fig. 5. increased toward the Kuroshio, Trichodesmium became more abundant. When spring data between 1994 and 1996 were combined, a statistically significant relationship was found between temperature at 10 m depth and integrated Trichodesmium abundance (Fig. 6(a)). The positive correlation existed even when data points with zero value were excluded from the regression. However, temperature alone was unable to explain all distribution patterns observed in the East China Sea. For the fall-type distribution, no relationship with water temperature could be established (Fig. 6(b)). The population density in the Kuroshio was 30 times less than that in the coastal zone while water temperature in Kuroshio remained warmer than 28°C (Figs. 4 and 5). Similarly, temperature alone failed to explain the observed seasonal cycle of Trichodesmium in Kuroshio (Fig. 2). The Kuroshio water near Taiwan is constantly warmer than 24°C year-round. Thus, it is surprising to see that Trichodesmium abundance went through such an dramatic change in a year. Of course, *Trichodesmium*'s ability in fixing nitrogen is vulnerable to turbulence (Carpenter and Price, 1976), and the strong mixing in winter might cause *Trichodesmium* abundance to decrease in the warm Kuroshio (Fig. 2(c)). However, a rapid decrease in *Trichodesmium* abundance was noticed in fall when water temperature was still high and the mixing depth was shallower than 50 m (Fig. 2). Marumo and Asaoka (1974) proposed that a substance in coastal water is essential for the growth of *Trichodesmium*. Because of this substance, dense *Trichodesmium* populations formed at several locations along the course of Kuroshio where the mixing with coastal waters took place (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974). In our study area, the most intensive mixing between the coastal water and the Kuroshio current occurs in winter when part of the Kuroshio flows onto the East China Sea continental shelf (Gong et al., 1997). As a result, ample amount of this substance enters the Kuroshio zone during winter, and supports *Trichodesmium* growth in spring when mixing depth decreases. Later, the active growth in spring and summer deprived this substance from Kuroshio which in turn retarded *Trichodesmium* growth and caused the standing crop to shrink in fall (Figs. 2 and 4). Meanwhile, temperature in the coastal zone was quite warm in fall, and a continuous supply of this substance stimulated the growth of *Trichodesmium*, caused its biomass to increase, and created an environment favoring bloom formation. The phenomenon of a coastal substance in controlling *Trichodesmium* distribution was further supported by observations made on a cruise that covered the entire East China Sea in 1992. High trichome concentrations were mainly found in an area influenced by the Yangtze River (Chen et al., 1996; Gong et al., 1996). However, there is no direct evidence to confirm such a relationship in East China Sea, and other mechanisms, such as the grazing by toxin-resistant harpacticoid copepods (O’Neil and Roman, 1994), cannot be excluded as possible causes for the observed distribution patterns. The amount of new nitrogen introduced to East China Sea and Kuroshio by *Trichodesmium* can be estimated from trichome concentration and nitrogen fixation rate. According to measurements conducted in Kuroshio near southern Japan (Saino and Hattori, 1980), an averaged acetylene reduction rate was 0.7 pmole ethylene trichome\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) in samples containing only individual trichomes. If we accept the theoretical 3 : 1 acetylene reduction to nitrogen fixation conversion ratio (Capone, 1993), and the fact that *Trichodesmium* fixes nitrogen only in sunlight hours (assumed to be 12 h per day, Saino and Hattori, 1980), nitrogen fixation rate in the Kuroshio/East China Sea region would be 5.6 pmol N trichome\(^{-1}\) d\(^{-1}\). Based on *Trichodesmium* abundance observed at our study area, nitrogen fixation rate in Kuroshio was estimated as between 0.1 and 59 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 2). This estimate was extremely close to the 34 \( \pm \) 11 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) nitrogen fixation input required to maintain the depletion of \(^{15}\)N observed at 100 m depth in the same region (Liu et al., 1996). Using the same computational procedure, if *Trichodesmium* nitrogen fixation was not suppressed by the elevated nitrate supply in the upwelling region, the resultant nitrogen input would range from 0.3 to 34 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) (Table 2). When the nitrogen fixation rate was converted to primary productivity using the Redfield ratio (C : N ratio by atoms = 106 : 16; Carpenter, 1983b), *Trichodesmium* Table 2 Estimated Trichodesmium nitrogen fixation rate and its contribution to primary production in southern East China Sea

Since the \( f \)-ratio in Kuroshio ranged from 0.09 to 0.25 (Gong, unpublished), Trichodesmium may contribute up to 25% of the local new production. In contrast, the fraction of primary production supported by nitrogen fixation in the upwelling zone was much less (Table 2). However, because Trichodesmium blooms were never encountered during our survey, the above estimate reflected nitrogen input under non-bloom conditions. Recent evidence indicated that nitrogen fixation rate in a Trichodesmium bloom can reach a very high level at 150 pg N trichome−1 h−1 (129 pmol N trichome−1 d−1), presumably due to colony formation (Carpenter and Capone, 1992). In August 1990, high densities of Trichodesmium at \( 3.7 \times 10^4 \) trichomes l−1 was observed at a station in the mid-shelf zone of East China Sea (Chen, 1992). If this bloom extended from sea surface to a depth of merely 1 m, the depth-integrated biomass would reach \( 3.7 \times 10^7 \) trichomes m−2. When the nitrogen fixation rate under bloom condition was applied, Trichodesmium would support a primary productivity of 31.5 mmol C m−2 d−1, much higher than total primary productivity normally measured in the Kuroshio zone. Effects of Lake Size on Nutrient Availability in the Mixed Layer during Summer Stratification E.J. Fee, R.E. Hecky, G.W. Regehr, L.L. Hendzel, and P. Wilkinson Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Central and Arctic Region, Freshwater Institute, 501 University Crescent, Winnipeg, MB R3T 2N6, Canada Fee, E.J., R.E. Hecky, G.W. Regehr, L.L. Hendzel, and P. Wilkinson. 1994. Effects of lake size on nutrient availability in the mixed layer during summer stratification. Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. 51: 2756–2768. Fluxes to the summer mixed layer of N, Si, and P were estimated in a size series of northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes. Increasing turbulence caused upward fluxes through the thermocline to increase with lake size for nutrients that increased in concentration below the thermocline (soluble reactive Si, total inorganic N, and NO_3^−; but not total N or any form of P). Precipitation and terrestrial runoff were equally important sources of N and P in all but very small lakes (<100 ha), where precipitation supplied much more than runoff. Runoff was the only important source of Si, except in very large lakes (> 100 000 ha) where mixing through the thermocline was important. N_2-fixation was unimportant except in intermediate-sized lakes (700–2000 ha). Si fluxes nearly equaled phytoplankton requirements, but N and P were below requirements, and recycling within the mixed layer must be the most important source of these nutrients. N and P deficits increased progressively with lake size, implying that the efficiency of nutrient recycling increased with lake size; mixed layers in large lakes are more turbulent and thicker than in small lakes and these processes increase the probability of nutrient regeneration within the mixed layer. Les flux de N, de Si et de P vers la couche de mélange estivale ont été estimés dans des lacs de différentes tailles du Bouclier canadien dans le nord-ouest de l’Ontario. Une turbulence accrue donne lieu à une augmentation proportionnelle à la taille des lacs des flux ascendants dans la thermocline dans le cas des éléments nutritifs dont la concentration augmente sous la thermocline (Si réactif soluble, N inorganique total, et NO_3^−); mais non le N total et aucune forme de P). Les précipitations et le ruissellement de surface étaient des sources de N et de P d’égale importance dans tous les lacs, sauf dans les très petits (<100 ha), où la contribution des précipitations étaient beaucoup plus importante à cet égard. Le ruissellement était la seule source importante de Si, sauf sans les très grands lacs (> 100 000 ha), où le mélange dans la thermocline apportait une contribution importante. La fixation du N_2 n’était pas importante sauf dans les lacs de taille intermédiaire (700–2 000 ha). Les flux de Si satisfaisaient presque les besoins du phytoplancton alors que ceux de N et de P étaient insuffisants, le recyclage dans la couche de mélange assurant probablement le principal apport de ces deux derniers éléments. Les carences en N et en P allaient en s’accroissant avec la taille des lacs, ce qui implique que la contribution du recyclage des éléments nutritifs s’accroît avec la taille des lacs; en effet, les couches de mélange des grands lacs sont plus turbulentes et plus épaisses que celles des petits lacs, ce qui accroît les possibilités de régénération des éléments nutritifs dans la couche de mélange. Received September 21, 1993 Accepted July 12, 1994 (J12098) Reçu le 21 septembre 1993 Accepté le 12 juillet 1994 When Johnson and Vallentyne (1971) introduced the Experimental Lakes Area (ELA) program in the scientific literature, they clearly recognized that extrapolation of results obtained from the observation and manipulation of very small lakes to larger, more economically important ones was a fundamental assumption of ELA’s design. They presented several examples of how a lake’s size might affect critical limnological processes and stated that these “... must be taken into account in any extrapolation.” Yet for nearly two decades, ELA results have been extrapolated to larger lakes without any explicit consideration of such effects. The Northwest Ontario Lake Size Series (NOLSS) program (Fee and Hecky 1992) was designed to remedy this deficiency; specifically, the purpose of NOLSS is to investigate physical gradients associated with lake size and to determine their biological significance. In an initial NOLSS publication, Fee et al. (1992) reported that annual rates of phytoplankton photosynthesis (PP) per unit of lake surface area (i.e., areal PP) increased progressively with lake size simply because larger lakes were ice free for longer periods and had thicker mixed layers than small lakes. In contrast, these authors showed that annual rates of PP per unit volume of the mixed layer (volumetric PP) varied with lake size in a bell-shaped pattern, i.e., rates in the smallest and largest lakes (29 ha ELA Lake 373 and 8 × 10^6 ha Lake Superior, respectively) were low and similar, whereas midsized lakes had rates nearly an order of magnitude greater. Fee et al. (1992) hypothesized that this pattern resulted from systematic changes of turbulence and water temperature with increasing lake size. According to this hypothesis, the increasing intensity of turbulence with 1This is one in a series of papers describing work of the Freshwater Institute Science Laboratory on a lake-size series in Northwest Ontario. It is also a contribution to the series honoring the 25th anniversary of the Experimental Lakes Area. lake size (Ward 1977; Quay et al. 1980) stimulates volumetric PP by increasing nutrient availability in the mixed layer, but decreasing water temperature with increasing lake size (Fee and Hecky 1992) simultaneously depresses it; the opposite effects of these two gradients on PP results in optimum conditions for PP in midsized lakes. This paper investigates one of the basic assumptions of this hypothesis: viz., that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP by making nutrients more available within the mixed layer. It is well documented that algal growth and biomass in Canadian Shield lakes is limited by nutrients; more specifically, PP is primarily phosphorus (P) limited (Schindler 1977; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1987; Hecky et al. 1993; and especially S. Guildford and L. Hendzel, Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Winnipeg, MB, unpublished data for the NOLSS lakes). Theoretically, turbulence should be positively and causally related to nutrient availability in the mixed layer because: (1) more turbulent mixed layers retain particles longer, and thus recycle nutrients more effectively and (2) turbulence is the physical process responsible for the upward transport of nutrients through the summer thermocline. The second mechanism is more conditional than the first, however, because the turbulent (mixing) flux through the thermocline is not solely a function of the intensity of turbulence. That is, the flux of a substance S through a plane at depth z is \[ \text{Flux} = K_z \frac{dS}{dz} \] where \( K_z \) is the coefficient of vertical eddy diffusion (i.e., turbulence). Hence, turbulence can result in a net upward flux to the mixed layer only if the concentration of S increases with depth in the region of the thermocline. In this paper, we examine all major nutrient fluxes to the summer mixed layer in a size series of hydrologically and morphometrically similar lakes, during the period 1986-1991. Our purpose is to compare the magnitude of the only flux that depends explicitly on lake size, the turbulence-mediated upward flux through the summer thermocline, with fluxes that are independent of lake size: precipitation, terrestrial runoff, and N\(_2\)-fixation. We then assess the ecological importance of these fluxes by comparing them with the nutrient requirements of algae residing in the mixed layer. Study Sites Table 1 summarizes morphometric features of the study lakes and defines morphometric symbols used throughout the text. All the lakes are located on the Canadian Shield in northwestern Ontario, have water renewal times >5 yr, and are deep enough to fully stratify during the summer. Except for Lakes Nipigon and Superior, whose basins are sparsely populated, there are no permanent residents in the drainage basins of the lakes. More detailed descriptions are given by Fee and Hecky (1992) and Fee et al. (1992). Methods Unless otherwise stated, field and laboratory methods follow Fee et al. (1989) and Stainton et al. (1977). Temperature-depth stratification was measured with an electronic temperature logger (R. Brancker Research Ltd., Ottawa, ON; 1 sample·s\(^{-1}\), precision of depth sensor ~0.05 m) that was lowered at a rate of ~0.5 m·s\(^{-1}\). This instrument was calibrated on several occasions with a manual resistance thermometer accurate to 0.1°C. The planar thermocline depth is defined as that depth where the rate of change of temperature with depth is greatest (normally >1°C·m\(^{-1}\)). The coefficient of eddy diffusivity, \( K_z \), was estimated using Ward's (1977) equation \[ K_z = 4.9 \times 10^{-12} \frac{g \sqrt{A_0}}{N} \] where g is the gravitational acceleration constant (9.81 m·s\(^{-2}\)), \( A_0 \) is the lake surface area, and N is the Brunt-Väisälä frequency: \[ N = \sqrt{\frac{d\rho}{dz} \cdot \frac{g}{\rho}} \] where \( \rho \) is the density of water. In oligotrophic Canadian Shield waters, \( \rho \) can be assumed to be solely a function of temperature (Quay et al. 1980) and we calculated it using Benson and Krause's (1980) equation \[ \rho = \exp(-0.589581 + 326.785/T - 45284.1/T^2) \] where T is \( ^0K \). Units throughout are metres and seconds, except for \( \rho \) which has units of grams per cubic centimetre. Water chemistry depth profiles were determined twice: once at the beginning and again at the end of summer stratification (mid-June and late August, except in Trout Lake and Lake Nipigon, where corresponding temperature stratification conditions occurred in early July and mid-September); chemistry profiles were not measured on Orange Lake or Lake Superior. A PVC Van Dorn bottle was used to collect water samples, which were transported to the laboratory in polyethylene bottles precleaned with dilute HCl, followed by three rinses of distilled water, and then air-dried. The following forms of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and silicon (Si) were measured: NO\(_3^-\) + NO\(_2^-\); NO\(_2^-\) (which was below the limit of detection everywhere); NH\(_4^+\); total dissolved N

Total inorganic N (TIN = \( NO_3^- + NO_2^- + NH_4^+ \)), total P (TP = TDP + SPP), and total N (TN = TDN + SPN) were obtained arithmetically. Orthophosphate (\( PO_4^{3-} \)) is undetectable in these waters (Stainton 1980). Turbulence-mediated nutrient fluxes up through the thermocline (mass\(\cdot\)m\(^{-2}\)\(\cdot\)d\(^{-1}\)) were multiplied by the ratio of the area of the lake at the depth of the thermocline (\( A_{th} \)) to the surface area of the lake (\( A_0 \)) (Table 2); this renders them directly comparable with other fluxes to the mixed layer (precipitation, terrestrial runoff, and N\(_2\)-fixation) and to the nutrient requirements of phytoplankton, which were based on the rate of phytoplankton photosynthesis per square metre of lake surface, corrected for the diminution of lake volume with depth (Fee 1980). Chemical concentrations were not measured in Orange Lake or Lake Superior; mixing fluxes thus cannot be calculated for these lakes directly. Mixing fluxes in Orange Lake were estimated by interpolating linearly (lake surface area being the independent variable) from those measured in Green and Linge Lakes. Because Lake Superior is the largest member of the size series, this method cannot be used and mixing fluxes are not available for this lake. The N, P, and Si requirements of phytoplankton residing in the mixed layer were estimated by dividing the rate of PP (mol C\(\cdot\)m\(^{-2}\)\(\cdot\)d\(^{-1}\), daily average for the period June 1 – August 31, corrected for the diminution of lake volume with depth, Fee 1980; data summarized by Fee et al. 1992) by the ratios of the concentrations of these nutrients to the concentration of carbon (C) in suspended particulate matter. For example, the amount of P needed to match the C fixed in photosynthesis is \[ \text{P}_{\text{required}} = \frac{\text{PP}_{\text{areal}}}{C : P_{\text{particulate}}} \] Suspended C, N, and P were determined on integrated (0–3 m) water samples collected every 3 wk during the summer of 1990. Suspended Si samples were collected in the same way, but in 1991 and 1992; they were analyzed using the method of Paasche (1973) modified by digesting filters in NaOH for a longer period (2 h). Bulk precipitation (rainfall plus accumulated dryfall) was collected after each significant rainfall event from a collector on the island in ELA Lake 240. Rainfall volume and chemical composition data collected there were assumed to apply to all the studied lakes; this is in agreement with the Hydrological Atlas of Canada (1978), which shows that the NOLSS and ELA areas (150 km apart) receive the same annual wet precipitation. In fact, similar total summer rainfall volumes fell at Red Lake, Ontario, which is near the center of the NOLSS study area, during this study (Fig. 1, average ratio for the 6 yr period = 1.04). Measurements were made with a modification of Flett et al.’s (1976) glass syringe incubation method (Hendzel et al. 1994). In situ N₂-fixation rates were calculated from acetylene production rates using Flett et al.’s (1976) average ratio of 1 mol of N₂ fixed for every 3 mol of ethylene produced. These were converted to daily areal rates by assuming that irradiances suitable for N₂-fixation at the measured rate occurred throughout the mixed layer for 10 h. Results The largest nutrient concentration gradients occurred deep in the hypolimnia of small lakes (top three panels in the left columns of Fig. 2 and 3); gradients were much smaller in larger lakes (right column of panels in Fig. 2 and 3). However, mixing fluxes through the thermocline depend only on concentration gradients at the depth of the thermocline (Equation (1)), and there was no obvious relationship between gradients at this depth and lake size (Table 2). Thus, lake-to-lake differences in the upward flux of individual nutrients through the thermocline depend almost entirely on \( K_z \), which was more than two orders of magnitude greater in the largest lake (Nipigon) than in the smallest (ELA Lake 373) (Table 2). Fluxes increased progressively with lake size for those nutrients that increased in concentration with depth in the region of the thermocline (NO₃⁻, TIN, and SRSi) but were nil for nutrients that had zero or negative gradients (TN, TDP, TP). Over a 21-yr period, the summer mixed layer of ELA Lake 239 received similar amounts of TN and TP from precipitation and terrestrial runoff (Fig. 4). There was always much more TIN and NO₃⁻ in precipitation than in runoff, but runoff was by far the most important source of Si. In 1990, upward mixing through the thermocline was an important source of nutrients (compared with precipitation and runoff) only in lakes >1000 ha (Table 3). The amount of N supplied by N₂-fixation was much less than that supplied by precipitation and runoff except in intermediate-sized lakes; why higher N₂-fixation rates occurred in these lakes is unclear, because other fluxes of N to them were not unusually low. Interannually, fluxes from precipitation and terrestrial runoff varied by about the same amount as did nutrient concentration gradients in the thermocline of Lake 239 (Fig. 5); the coefficients of variation of NO₃⁻ in precipitation and of concentration gradients of NO₃⁻ in the Lake 239 thermocline were both 40%. Figure 5 also shows that in 1990 (the only year for which we have the chemistry depth profile data required to estimate vertical mixing fluxes in the NOLSS lakes) vertical concentration gradients in Lake 239 were unusually low. If interannual variations of chemical concentration gradients in Lake 239 also occur in larger lakes, then mixing fluxes would be about double those given in Table 2 in an average year, and up to three times greater in high years. In 1990, fluxes of N and P to the mixed layer fell far short of phytoplankton requirements (Table 3 and left column of panels in Fig. 6), but the deficit of Si was slight. Discussion Turbulent mixing through the thermocline, the only nutrient flux to the mixed layer that is explicitly dependent on lake size, supplied less TN and TP than did those fluxes that are independent of lake size (precipitation, terrestrial runoff, N\(_2\)-fixation; Fig. 6). Mixing supplied more of some forms of N (NO\(_3^-\) and TIN) and of SRSi in larger than in smaller lakes (Table 3), but terrestrial runoff more than made up for the SRSi that turbulence failed to supply in small lakes. Thus, the only mixing fluxes of potential ecological importance are of NO\(_3^-\) and TIN. Although N plays an important role in determining phytoplankton community composition (Schindler 1977), it rarely limits algal biomass in unperturbed Canadian Shield lakes (Hecky and Kilham 1988). We, therefore, conclude that the turbulence-mediated upward flux of nutrients through the summer thermocline was an insignificant component of mixed-layer nutrient budgets in all sizes of Canadian Shield lakes in 1990. We did not measure concentrations of PO\(_4^{3-}\), the form of P most readily assimilated by phytoplankton, because standard chemical methods for measuring it always overestimate actual concentrations in Canadian Shield lakes (Stainton 1980). Moreover, when special radiochemical methods have been used to measure it, concentrations in these lakes were always minute (<0.003 \( \mu \)mol·L\(^{-1} \); Levine and Schindler 1980). Nevertheless, if PO\(_4^{3-}\) did increase in concentration with depth in the thermoclines of the lakes we studied, we may have missed an important source of this critical element. We obtained an upper bound on the magnitude of this flux by assuming that concentrations increase from 0 in the mixed layer to the highest summer values ever measured in the hypolimnia of unperturbed northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes (0.003 \( \mu \)mol·L\(^{-1} \); Levine and Schindler, 1980) over a distance of 1 m in all the lakes. These extremely generous assumptions yield upward (mixing) fluxes of P on the order of 0.002 \( \mu \)mol·m\(^{-2}\)·d\(^{-1} \), which amounts to only ~0.001% of the amount of P that phytoplankton living in the mixed layer require. We thus confidently conclude that the upward flux of PO\(_4^{3-}\) through the thermocline is insignificant in Canadian Shield lakes. None of the foregoing conclusions depend critically on our use of Equation (2) to estimate \( K_z \), which is a statistical fit to the results of Mortimer (1941), Jassby and Powell (1975), Hutchinson (1957), Hesslein and Quay (1973), and Ward (1977). Two of these papers (Mortimer’s and Hutchinson’s), in turn, summarize results from many other independent studies. A possible objection to these results, however, is that with one exception they are all based on measurements of the rate at which heat moved downward through the thermocline. The exception was Hesslein and Quay (1973), who found that in a very small, deep lake (ELA Lake 227; \( A_0 = 5 \) ha, \( z_m = 10 \) m) \( K_z \) as determined by measuring the transport of a dissolved material (radon gas) was much smaller than \( K_z \) as determined by measuring the transport of heat. This happened because turbulence was so low that transport was almost entirely the result of molecular diffusion, and heat has a higher coefficient of molecular conductivity than radon gas. Because all of our lakes are much larger than Lake 227, they have \( K_z \) values substantially greater than the molecular conductivity of heat, and this cannot be a problem here. Moreover, if \( K_z \) were smaller than the values we derived from Equation (2), vertical fluxes would be even smaller than those we calculated, which we have already concluded to be insignificant. Finally, because concentration gradients of all forms of P in the region of the thermocline were negligible, our conclusion that vertical fluxes of this critical element were nil in all lake sizes is completely independent of \( K_z \). Figure 6 shows that phytoplankton living in the mixed layer required much more P and N than all of the fluxes measured in 1990. The deficit of supply relative to demand was notably greater for P than for N, further confirming that P is the most limiting nutrient in Canadian Shield lakes (Schindler 1977, 1988; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1988; Levine and Schindler 1992; Hecky et al. 1993; S. Guildford and L. Hendzel, unpublished data). Some might object Supply/Demand Fig. 6. But Hecky et al. (1993) concluded that this was not a significant problem in Canadian Shield lakes with water residence times longer than a few months. Moreover, basing estimates of algal nutrient requirements on the Redfield ratios (106 for C/P and 6.6 for C/N; Redfield et al. 1963), which are widely accepted as the elemental composition of average algal cells, increases the gap between supply and demand because the C/P and C/N ratios of particles in our lakes were uniformly greater than the Redfield ratios (Table 3). Thus, our use of atomic ratios in particulate matter to estimate the nutrient requirements is, if anything, conservative. FIG. 7. June–August mean dissolved inorganic C (DIC) concentrations in the mixed layer and C content of profundal sediments in northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes. Another possible problem with our approach is that we assume that Fee et al.’s (1992) \(^{14}\)C-based PP values estimate daily net C fixation into particles. We emphasize that our use of the term “net” is distinct from another common use of this term, i.e., the amount of material exported from the primary trophic level during an entire growing season (stored in sediments, flushed out of the lake, or converted into the flesh of higher trophic levels). We make no assumption about what happens to particles over periods longer than a day. Bower et al. (1987) showed that in an ELA whole-lake \(^{14}\)C experiment, Fee et al.’s (1992) PP method closely approximated net daily incorporation of C into particles; all losses of \(^{14}\)C from particles occurred at night, and these losses averaged only 8% of the daytime rate of incorporation of inorganic C into particulate matter (range 3–17%, \(n = 13\)). Essentially, we explicitly ignore this small and variable correction, and assume that the \(^{14}\)C method used by Fee et al. (1992) yields estimates of daily net particulate C fixation; Peterson (1978) reported that this is true for rapidly growing algal cultures. The final critical basic assumption for our analysis is that all major nutrient fluxes to the mixed layer were measured. One potential nutrient source that we did not measure is that from epilimnion sediments. However, studies at ELA have repeatedly demonstrated that epilimnion sediments return little or no P to the water column (\(^{32}\)P measurements: Schindler et al. 1975; Levine et al. 1986; mass balance calculations: Schindler et al. 1973, 1987; Levine and Schindler 1989; porewater gradient measurements: Schindler et al. 1977; L. Hendzel, unpublished data). Levine and Schindler (1989) did find that littoral sediments supplied N to the mixed layer, but as mentioned above, N rarely limits phytoplankton biomass in Canadian Shield lakes. Moreover, Levine and Schindler (1992) showed that the N returned to the water column from epilimnetic sediments was almost entirely derived from materials recently deposited at the sediment–water interface, rather than from deep within the sediment itself; in our view, this constitutes nutrient recycling within the mixed layer. We thus conclude that Fig. 6 can be accepted at face value, and that fluxes of N and P to the mixed layer were a small fraction of the physiological requirements of phytoplankton in 1990. Indeed, these fluxes would be capable of meeting phytoplankton needs only in small lakes and if the most generous assumptions about supply and demand are made. The major implication is that recycling within the mixed layer must be the major source of N and P for algae living there. This is scarcely a new or surprising conclusion. Harrison (1980, and see references therein) showed that external inputs of N, P, and Si to the sea could account for <1% of the amounts required by phytoplankton, and he concluded that recycling supplied the remainder. In fresh water, Levine and Schindler (1980) found that in an unfertilized, stratified ELA lake (Lake 302S; \(A_0 = 10.9\) ha, \(z_m = 10.6\) m) an average P atom recycled through epilimnetic seston 17 times prior to being lost from the mixed layer, and Levine et al. (1986, p. 376) stated that “... the predominant source of phosphate for phytoplankton in the epilimnion is not external supply, but recycling.” This result has been corroborated by so many independent studies (see Planas and Hecky 1984, and references therein) that it would have been extremely surprising if our results contradicted it. Figure 6 illustrates what may be our single most important result, viz., the fraction of phytoplankton nutrient requirements accounted for by all estimated fluxes to the mixed layer systematically decreases with increasing lake size. That is, nutrient recycling within the mixed layer supplies a progressively increasing fraction of phytoplankton nutrient requirements as lake size increases. This is logical, because both the intensity of turbulence within the mixed layer and the thickness of the mixed layer increase with lake size. As a consequence, mixed-layer particle residence times increase with lake size; this increases the probability that particle-bound nutrients will be recycled within the mixed layer rather than being lost to the sediments. A lower bound on the magnitude of this effect can be derived using Hesslein et al.’s (1980) value of 0.18 m·d\(^{-1}\) for the settling rate of particles from the mixed layer of ELA Lake 224 (\(A_0 = 25.9\) ha, \(z_m = 27\) m). Applying this figure to all lake sizes, it would take 33 d for settling to remove all particles from the mixed layer of ELA Lake 373 (\(z_{th} = 6\) m) compared with 72 d in Trout Lake (\(z_{th} = 13\) m). However, because large lakes have much more turbulent mixed layers than small ones, the actual difference in particle residence times in large versus small lakes is undoubtedly even greater. The percent organic C in deep-water sediments declines in a strikingly regular fashion with increasing lake size (Fig. 7). This result strongly supports our conclusion that the rate of nutrient recycling within the mixed layer increases with increasing lake size. The longer that particles are retained in the mixed layer, the more likely it is that the C they contain will be respired back to CO\(_2\) and lost to the atmosphere rather than falling through the thermocline and accumulating in deep-water sediments. We do not believe that recycling is the only process responsible for producing this pattern. Indeed, such regularity is probably the product of many processes acting in concert (e.g., longer retention in the mixed layer, increasing total depth of the water column, decreasing terrestrial influence, etc.). Nevertheless, it is fully consonant with our conclusion that large lakes recycle nutrients more efficiently than small ones. The greater efficiency of nutrient recycling in the mixed layer in large than in small lakes has important implications for Fee's (1979) theory that the rate of nutrient recycling is a function of basin morphometry. He found that in small ELA lakes, the area of epilimnion sediments (\(A_e\)) divided by the volume of the epilimnion (\(V_e\)) was strongly correlated with rates of volumetric PP. He demonstrated that, if all other factors are equal, \(A_e/V_e\) is mathematically equivalent to the probability of retention of particles in the mixed layer and thus parameterized the rate of nutrient recycling. He cautioned that this might not be true in larger lakes, where processes that are negligible in small lakes could affect nutrient recycling. Our results bear out this prediction; as lakes increase in size, the increasing intensity of turbulence within the mixed layer and the increasing thickness of the mixed layer both retard sedimentation losses through the thermocline, thereby increasing mixed layer particle residence time. Consequently, a large lake with a low \(A_e/V_e\) value and a small lake with a high \(A_e/V_e\) value could have the same mixed layer particle residence times and similar rates of nutrient recycling. An important corollary is that large and small lakes with similar \(A_e/V_e\) values should respond differently to the same external P loading. Productivity should be higher in the large lake because of its higher rate of nutrient recycling. These results lend strong support to Margalef's (1974) theory that physical energy levels directly control food-web structures and the biogeochemical characteristics of water bodies. The largest nutrient concentration gradients occurred deep in the water column of small lakes (Fig. 2 and 3); in contrast, large lakes had relatively well-mixed hypolimnia with maximum gradients at or just below the thermocline. This difference is probably the result of several processes: (1) Internal waves, which are the primary source of hypolimnetic turbulence, are significant only in lakes with surface areas >1000 ha (Boyce 1974); thus, in small lakes, nutrients from particles remineralized near the bottom of the water column move upward very slowly compared with larger lakes. (2) Sediment focussing is very important in small lakes (Anderson et al. 1987) and causes particles that fall through the thermocline to move rapidly to great depths. (3) Because small lakes have shallow mixed layers, significant quantities of light penetrate below their thermoclines (Fee et al. 1991), permitting large algal populations to develop deep in their water columns (Fee 1976). These algal populations intercept nutrients diffusing up from below and prevent them from reaching the thermocline. Schindler and Nighswander (1970) and Bayley et al. (1992) reported that precipitation was the major source of N and P to Canadian Shield lakes. However, their conclusion was based on results obtained from the study of quite small lakes. Our results (Fig. 6) indicate that this does not apply to Canadian Shield lakes >300 ha, where fluxes of N and P from terrestrial runoff and precipitation were very similar in magnitude. Unlike N and P, there was virtually no Si in precipitation, and mixing supplied substantial quantities of this nutrient only in very large lakes (Fig. 6). However, terrestrial runoff of Si was large, particularly in small and midsized lakes, and the sum of all the fluxes that we measured apparently match phytoplankton requirements. There must, therefore, be some reason, other than a lack of supply, for why diatoms are unimportant components of the summer phytoplankton community in small, stratified Canadian Shield lakes (Kling and Holmgren 1972; Findlay and Kasian 1990). Again, the most likely explanation is based on the low mixed-layer turbulence and shallow mixed-layer depths in small lakes. Theoretically, the higher specific gravity of diatoms gives them a selective advantage over nonsinking or weakly motile competitors because by sinking they increase the rate at which they contact dissolved nutrients (by thinning the nutrient-depleted boundary layer that surrounds them: Hutchinson 1967; Margalef 1974; Titman and Kilham 1976). This strategy works well in large lakes, where high turbulence and deep mixed layers keep cells from being rapidly lost by sedimentation through the thermocline. Diatoms are also well represented in small, unstratified lakes, which lack a hypolimnion sedimentation trap altogether (Kling and Holmgren 1972). However, this strategy apparently fails in small, stratified lakes where shallow mixed layers and relatively stable water columns lead to rapid removal of sinking cells from the mixed layer. Conclusion The increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size acted in concert with positive concentration gradients of NO\(_3^-\), TDN, and SRSi in the region of the thermocline to result in more of these nutrients being transported upwards through the thermoclines in large than in small lakes (Table 2). These nutrients, however, rarely limit phytoplankton growth in Canadian Shield lakes. Because concentration gradients of P, the nutrient that does limit algal growth in Canadian Shield lakes, were nil in the region of the thermocline in all of these lakes (Fig. 2 and 3; Table 2), upward fluxes of P were essentially zero in all lake sizes. Our results support Fee et al.'s (1992) hypothesis that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP. It does this by acting in concert with the increasing depth of the mixed layer to cause particles to be retained in the mixed layer longer, thus increasing the probability that nutrients will be recycled within the mixed layer rather than lost to the sediments. Our results do not, however, rule out the possibility that the greater rates of volumetric PP in midsized lakes reported by Fee et al. (1992) are caused by lake-to-lake differences of external P loading. That is, although our results show that, all other things being equal, higher turbulence and thicker mixed layers enhance nutrient recycling and lead to higher rates of areal PP in larger lakes, the approach we have taken of using runoff and precipitation data measured in the basin of one small ELA lake to estimate P loading in all the other lakes has inherent inaccuracies (Fee and Hecky 1992). External P loading within this lake-size series could vary enough to explain the observed differences of volumetric PP. Nevertheless, Fee et al. (1992) showed that it is unlikely that areal PP, which theoretically sets potential yields of higher trophic levels, is the result of lake-to-lake differences in external P loading. Our main conclusion, that the probability of regeneration of nutrients within the mixed layer increases with lake size, has an important corollary: external nutrient loads should be converted into higher trophic levels, including especially valued organisms such as fish, more efficiently in large than in small lakes. This prediction is in harmony with Nixon's (1988) conclusion that the greatest standing crops of benthos and highest fish yields come from the most energetic marine environments. He further noted that, as we found in large lakes, sediments from these highly productive regions contained less C than did sediments from less energetic environments. His interpretation of these observations was also the same as ours, viz., that energetic mixed layers recycle nutrients more efficiently than less energetic ones. lake size (Ward 1977; Quay et al. 1980) stimulates volumetric PP by increasing nutrient availability in the mixed layer, but decreasing water temperature with increasing lake size (Fee and Hecky 1992) simultaneously depresses it; the opposite effects of these two gradients on PP results in optimum conditions for PP in midsized lakes. This paper investigates one of the basic assumptions of this hypothesis: viz., that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP by making nutrients more available within the mixed layer. It is well documented that algal growth and biomass in Canadian Shield lakes is limited by nutrients; more specifically, PP is primarily phosphorus (P) limited (Schindler 1977; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1987; Hecky et al. 1993; and especially S. Guildford and L. Hendzel, Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Winnipeg, MB, unpublished data for the NOLSS lakes). Theoretically, turbulence should be positively and causally related to nutrient availability in the mixed layer because: (1) more turbulent mixed layers retain particles longer, and thus recycle nutrients more effectively and (2) turbulence is the physical process responsible for the upward transport of nutrients through the summer thermocline. The second mechanism is more conditional than the first, however, because the turbulent (mixing) flux through the thermocline is not solely a function of the intensity of turbulence. That is, the flux of a substance S through a plane at depth z is \[ \text{Flux} = K_z \frac{dS}{dz} \] where \( K_z \) is the coefficient of vertical eddy diffusion (i.e., turbulence). Hence, turbulence can result in a net upward flux to the mixed layer only if the concentration of S increases with depth in the region of the thermocline. In this paper, we examine all major nutrient fluxes to the summer mixed layer in a size series of hydrologically and morphometrically similar lakes, during the period 1986-1991. Our purpose is to compare the magnitude of the only flux that depends explicitly on lake size, the turbulence-mediated upward flux through the summer thermocline, with fluxes that are independent of lake size: precipitation, terrestrial runoff, and N\(_2\)-fixation. We then assess the ecological importance of these fluxes by comparing them with the nutrient requirements of algae residing in the mixed layer. Study Sites Table 1 summarizes morphometric features of the study lakes and defines morphometric symbols used throughout the text. All the lakes are located on the Canadian Shield in northwestern Ontario, have water renewal times >5 yr, and are deep enough to fully stratify during the summer. Except for Lakes Nipigon and Superior, whose basins are sparsely populated, there are no permanent residents in the drainage basins of the lakes. More detailed descriptions are given by Fee and Hecky (1992) and Fee et al. (1992). Methods Unless otherwise stated, field and laboratory methods follow Fee et al. (1989) and Stainton et al. (1977). Temperature-depth stratification was measured with an electronic temperature logger (R. Brancker Research Ltd., Ottawa, ON; 1 sample·s\(^{-1}\), precision of depth sensor ~0.05 m) that was lowered at a rate of ~0.5 m·s\(^{-1}\). This instrument was calibrated on several occasions with a manual resistance thermometer accurate to 0.1°C. The planar thermocline depth is defined as that depth where the rate of change of temperature with depth is greatest (normally >1°C·m\(^{-1}\)). The coefficient of eddy diffusivity, \( K_z \), was estimated using Ward's (1977) equation \[ K_z = 4.9 \times 10^{-12} \frac{g \sqrt{A_0}}{N} \] where g is the gravitational acceleration constant (9.81 m·s\(^{-2}\)), \( A_0 \) is the lake surface area, and N is the Brunt-Väisälä frequency: \[ N = \sqrt{\frac{d\rho}{dz} \cdot \frac{g}{\rho}} \] where \( \rho \) is the density of water. In oligotrophic Canadian Shield waters, \( \rho \) can be assumed to be solely a function of temperature (Quay et al. 1980) and we calculated it using Benson and Krause's (1980) equation \[ \rho = \exp(-0.589581 + 326.785/T - 45284.1/T^2) \] where T is \( ^0K \). Units throughout are metres and seconds, except for \( \rho \) which has units of grams per cubic centimetre. Water chemistry depth profiles were determined twice: once at the beginning and again at the end of summer stratification (mid-June and late August, except in Trout Lake and Lake Nipigon, where corresponding temperature stratification conditions occurred in early July and mid-September); chemistry profiles were not measured on Orange Lake or Lake Superior. A PVC Van Dorn bottle was used to collect water samples, which were transported to the laboratory in polyethylene bottles precleaned with dilute HCl, followed by three rinses of distilled water, and then air-dried. The following forms of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and silicon (Si) were measured: NO\(_3^-\) + NO\(_2^-\); NO\(_2^-\) (which was below the limit of detection everywhere); NH\(_4^+\); total dissolved N

Total inorganic N (TIN = \( NO_3^- + NO_2^- + NH_4^+ \)), total P (TP = TDP + SPP), and total N (TN = TDN + SPN) were obtained arithmetically. Orthophosphate (\( PO_4^{3-} \)) is undetectable in these waters (Stainton 1980). Turbulence-mediated nutrient fluxes up through the thermocline (mass\(\cdot\)m\(^{-2}\)\(\cdot\)d\(^{-1}\)) were multiplied by the ratio of the area of the lake at the depth of the thermocline (\( A_{th} \)) to the surface area of the lake (\( A_0 \)) (Table 2); this renders them directly comparable with other fluxes to the mixed layer (precipitation, terrestrial runoff, and N\(_2\)-fixation) and to the nutrient requirements of phytoplankton, which were based on the rate of phytoplankton photosynthesis per square metre of lake surface, corrected for the diminution of lake volume with depth (Fee 1980). Chemical concentrations were not measured in Orange Lake or Lake Superior; mixing fluxes thus cannot be calculated for these lakes directly. Mixing fluxes in Orange Lake were estimated by interpolating linearly (lake surface area being the independent variable) from those measured in Green and Linge Lakes. Because Lake Superior is the largest member of the size series, this method cannot be used and mixing fluxes are not available for this lake. The N, P, and Si requirements of phytoplankton residing in the mixed layer were estimated by dividing the rate of PP (mol C\(\cdot\)m\(^{-2}\)\(\cdot\)d\(^{-1}\), daily average for the period June 1 – August 31, corrected for the diminution of lake volume with depth, Fee 1980; data summarized by Fee et al. 1992) by the ratios of the concentrations of these nutrients to the concentration of carbon (C) in suspended particulate matter. For example, the amount of P needed to match the C fixed in photosynthesis is \[ \text{P}_{\text{required}} = \frac{\text{PP}_{\text{areal}}}{C : P_{\text{particulate}}} \] Suspended C, N, and P were determined on integrated (0–3 m) water samples collected every 3 wk during the summer of 1990. Suspended Si samples were collected in the same way, but in 1991 and 1992; they were analyzed using the method of Paasche (1973) modified by digesting filters in NaOH for a longer period (2 h). Bulk precipitation (rainfall plus accumulated dryfall) was collected after each significant rainfall event from a collector on the island in ELA Lake 240. Rainfall volume and chemical composition data collected there were assumed to apply to all the studied lakes; this is in agreement with the Hydrological Atlas of Canada (1978), which shows that the NOLSS and ELA areas (150 km apart) receive the same annual wet precipitation. In fact, similar total summer rainfall volumes fell at Red Lake, Ontario, which is near the center of the NOLSS study area, during this study (Fig. 1, average ratio for the 6 yr period = 1.04). According to the Hydrological Atlas, Lakes Nipigon and Superior receive about 30% more wet precipitation than the ELA and NOLSS regions.
