tions needed to improve water quality (e.g., Christian and Thomas 2003) or assess implications of system changes on fisheries productivity (e.g., Mortazavi et al. 2000; Brock 2001) or other regional and global issues (Boyer and Howarth 2002).

Published and unpublished data obtained with similar methods (Fig. 1) suggest that N-cycling rates in Texas coastal waters are comparable to rates observed in hypereutrophic ecosystems such as Lake Maracaibo (Venezuela), Taihu Lake (China), and Old Woman Creek (tributary of Lake Erie), and higher than rates observed in the Mississippi River plume in the northern Gulf of Mexico and the Great Lakes. This result is not intuitive because tributary nutrient inputs are limited in arid coastal regions in south Texas. A recent summary of Gulf of Mexico estuarine benthic processes (Twilley et al. 1999) indicated that benthic fluxes of dissolved inorganic N compounds also are not sufficient to support observed primary production rates. An important question is: “What is the N source supporting high productivity and N cycling rates observed in these coastal ecosystems, which are often N limited?” Atmospheric N_2 fixation may be a major source of available N in these systems. For example, algal mats at the sediment–water interface are active regions for fixation and may provide N, which can be recycled in the system (Paerl and Zehr 2000). Although biological N fixation is important to the N cycle at regional and global scales, it has been not included or underrepresented in most ecological models (Vitousek et. al. 2002). Nitrogen fixation has not been studied thoroughly in Texas estuaries, but rates exceeded those of denitrification when examined in Laguna Madre (An et al. 2001). This process should be considered in conjunction with denitrification and other internal processes to evaluate its relative importance.

Nitrogen transformations and fate may relate to salinity in coastal ecosystems. A higher percentage of mineralized N is denitrified at the sediment–water interface in freshwater than in marine systems (Seitzinger 1988). Potential mechanisms include salinity-driven increases in NH_4^+ fluxes out of the sediments due to ion pairing of NH_4^+ with salt water anions (Gardner et al. 1991) and blocking of ion exchange sites by seawater cations (Seitzinger et al. 1991); inhibition of nitrification/denitrification by sulfide (Joye and Hollibaugh 1995); and effects on microorganism physiology (Rysgaard et al. 1999). DNRA is enhanced by sulfide- or sulfate-reducing bacteria (Rysgaard et al. 1996) and occurs in coastal regions (Sørensen 1978; Tobias et al. 2001), including the Laguna Madre (An and Gardner 2002).

In this paper, N flux and transformation processes are examined seasonally along the Texas coast, ranging from low-salinity river mouths and brackish Sabine Lake to the hypersaline Laguna Madre/Baffin Bay. Specific questions addressed are: (1) What are the relative rates of sediment N-transformation processes in Texas estuaries? (2) Do N transformations at the sediment–water interface reflect net fixation (source) or net denitrification (sink) for available N? (3) How do DNRA and other sediment–water N transformation rates and fluxes relate to salinity and redox conditions in these dynamic systems?

Site descriptions—The Texas coast (Fig. 2) is subtropical and characterized by shallow bays and lagoons with a substantial rainfall gradient from northeast to southwest along the coast (Solis and Powell 1999). Mean annual rainfall ranges from >140 cm at the Texas–Louisiana border to about 65 cm in the arid southern regions, where evaporation exceeds rainfall and causes high salinities in enclosed regions, such as the Laguna Madre. This range in rainfall and salinities makes the Texas coast a “natural laboratory” to investigate river input and salinity effects on N dynamics (sources, fluxes, transformations, and fate) in coastal environments. Most waters in the area are oxic because of wind

</page>

<page number="2">

mixing and shallow depths, but hypoxia occurs in southeastern Corpus Christi Bay and other areas where water residence times are long (about 5.5 months; Montagna and Kalke 1992; Ritter and Montagna 1999).

Laguna Madre Estuary (Fig. 2) is located south of Corpus Christi. It is the largest (by area) and longest of any Texas estuary and separated from the Gulf of Mexico by Padre Island. No major rivers or streams discharge into this system (Orlando et al. 1993). Upper Laguna Madre and Baffin Bay have a water residence time of about 1 yr and freshwater input is, on average, less than evaporation. About 65% of total freshwater discharged into the estuary is from direct precipitation (Orlando et al. 1993). Salinities are often >40 and can reach up to 60 (Buskey et al. 1998). Laguna Madre has been affected by Texas brown tide, a nuisance algal bloom persisting more than a decade (Buskey et al. 1998). The Texas brown tide organism, Aureomonas lagunensis, can use NH$_4^+$ or NO$_2^-$, but not NO$_3^-$, as an N source (DeYoe and Suttle 1994).

Sabine Lake is a shallow, brackish (mean salinity about 10) lake/tidal lagoon about 22.5 km long and 11.3 km wide. It is formed by the confluence of the Neches and Sabine Rivers, located on the Louisiana–Texas boundary, and drains about 130,000 km$^2$ of Texas and Louisiana into the Gulf of Mexico.

East Matagorda Bay is located between Matagorda and Galveston Bays (Fig. 2) and has little direct freshwater inflow except rainfall. Part of the Colorado River flows directly to the Gulf of Mexico, and its delta separates Matagorda and East Matagorda Bays. East Matagorda Bay is oriented in a southwest–northeast direction for about 32 km and has a width of about 6.5 km. It is enclosed on all sides with indirect access to small tributaries via the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway and with the Gulf of Mexico via Mitchell’s Cut, which is sometimes closed, at the northern end of the bay (Kraus and Militello 1999). Few studies have focused on this shallow (maximum depth <2 m), muddy bay, except for a survey of freshwater inflow effects on macrobenthos abundance (Montagna 2001).

The Nueces Estuary is a shallow, microtidal estuary near Corpus Christi (Fig. 2). It includes Corpus Christi Bay (average depth 3.6 m) and two secondary bays (Nueces Bay and Oso Bay), which average 2 m and 1 m in depth, respectively. The estuary is separated from the Gulf of Mexico by a barrier island and has exchange with the Gulf via Aransas Pass, a restricted inlet. The drainage basin is semi-arid but, like the other regions, subjected to occasional tropical storms and flood flows (Brock 2001). Sediment–water nutrient fluxes and denitrification rates were measured for this estuary and compared to results from the Guadalupe Estuary (Yoon and Benner 1992; Twilley et al. 1999), but N fixation was not measured. Indirect evidence suggested that DNRA may be important (Yoon and Benner 1992).

Methods

Continuous-flow experiments to quantify nutrient and gas fluxes were conducted on intact sediment cores after each sampling event. Characteristics of continuous-flow methodology have been described and compared to closed-system approaches (Kana et al. 1994; Miller-Way and Twilley 1996; An et al. 2001).

Bottom water at each station was collected for nutrient analysis and sediment core incubations. Undisturbed sediment cores (7.6 cm inner diameter, ca. 30 cm length; three per station) were collected from a boat using a coring device equipped with a polyvinyl chloride pipe handle and a one-way rubber valve (bathroom flush valve) to preserve core and overlying water integrity. After transport to the laboratory, an adjustable flow-through plunger with O-ring seal and Teflon inlet and outlet tubes was installed over each sediment core (Lavrentyev et al. 2000; An et al. 2001). Each continuous-flow chamber consisted of an intake water vessel, Teflon flow tubes, a peristaltic pump, temperature-controlled incubation bath, and sample-collection vessels. Water column depth over the sediment was maintained at about 5 cm to give a water volume of about 230 ml over each core. Sediment cores were placed in the incubation bath at in situ temperature, and bottom water from the site was passed continuously over the core surface at 1.2 ml min$^{-1}$. The bottom water was aerated, except for experiments from Corpus Christi Bay hypoxic sites in August 2002, to maintain oxic conditions. Cores were wrapped with aluminum foil to prevent light effects, except for one half of the cores from Laguna Madre/Baffin Bay and Sabine Lake, which were incubated in dim light. After 1 d of incubation to achieve steady state, triplicate inflow and outflow samples were collected once or twice daily for dissolved gas analysis by membrane inlet mass spectrometry (MIMS). Dissolved N$_2$, O$_2$, and Ar were measured with MIMS using methods (An et al. 2001) modified from Kana et al. (1994). Additional samples were collected for analysis of dissolved inorganic N (DIN) compounds. Nitrate and NO$_2^-$ were analyzed with a Lachat QuikChem 8000 FIA, and NH$_4^+$ concentration and isotopic content were measured by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC; Gardner et al. 1995a). Sediment flux was calculated for each compound on the basis of the concentration difference between inflow and outflow water, flow rate, and cross-sectional area (Lavrentyev et al. 2000).

Isotopic enrichment experiments were conducted to provide information needed to estimate N fixation, total denitrification, and DNRA rates (An et al. 2001). Inflow water was enriched with $^{15}$NO$_3^-$ (about 100 $\mu$L$^{-1}$ final concentration) after the second sampling day. Three different masses of N$_2$ gas produced by denitrification were measured using MIMS ($^{28}$N$_2$ from $^{14}$NO$_3^-$, 30N$_2$ from $^{15}$NO$_3^-$, and $^{29}$N$_2$ from $^{14}$NO$_3^-$ and $^{15}$NO$_3^-$; An et al. 2001). Concentration and atom% $^{15}$N-NH$_4^+$ were determined by HPLC (Gardner et al. 1995a). Nitrogen fixation and potential DNRA rates were calculated as described in An et al. (2001) and An and Gardner (2002), respectively. These extended experiments with $^{15}$NO$_3^-$ additions (An et al. 2001) were done on all cores except Laguna Madre in April and August 1999.

An additional $^{15}$NH$_4^+$ experiment was done on East Matagorda Bay sediments to examine uptake and release exchange of NH$_4^+$ at the sediment–water interface under conditions otherwise similar to the $^{15}$NO$_3^-$ addition experiments. Triplicate cores were collected, set up, and equilibrated as described above. Twenty micromoles per liter $^{15}$NH$_4^+$ plus

</page>

<page number="3">

100 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\) \(^{14}\)NO\(_3^-\) were added to the inflow water and measurements were conducted as described. Total NH\(_4^+\) uptake was calculated by measuring \(^{15}\)NH\(_4^+\) uptake (as the decrease of \(^{15}\)NH\(_4^+\) in the outflow vs. the inflow water) and dividing it by the \(^{15}\)NH\(_4^+\):total NH\(_4^+\) ratio in the outflow water. Total NH\(_4^+\) release was calculated as the difference between net NH\(_4^+\) flux and total NH\(_4^+\) uptake.

Sediment cores for microelectrode analysis were taken from Corpus Christi Bay during seasonal hypoxia in August 2002 and during norm-oxic conditions in April 2003. Cores were collected manually by SCUBA divers with care to minimize disturbance during collection, covered and clasped with fitted tops, and taken to the laboratory. Vertical (i.e., downcore) measurement steps were every 1 mm for the first 10 mm, then every 2 mm to 60 mm, and every 5 mm to 100 mm. Porewater O\(_2\) and \( \Sigma \)H\(_2\)S were measured simultaneously by anodic stripping voltammetry using solid-state potentiometric microelectrodes (Luther et al. 1998). Electroanalytical techniques were linear sweep and cyclic voltammetry, which was applied to the potential range from \(-0.1\) V to 2.1 V. Calibration of each electrode was based on the pilot ion method where Mn was the standardized ion (Brendel and Luther 1995).

Results

Physical and chemical characteristics of sampling sites.—Physical and chemical data for the different experimental sites are presented in Table 1. Water depths ranged from 0.4 to 2.2 m at most stations but were 2.7 to 3.0 m at the southeastern Corpus Christi Bay sites. Water temperatures ranged from 11\(^\circ\)C in the winter to 30\(^\circ\)C in summer. Near-bottom oxygen levels ranged from about 3 to 8 mg L\(^{-1}\) except for southeastern Corpus Christi Bay sites in August and one site in Baffin Bay, which had concentrations ranging from 0.1 to 2.3 mg L\(^{-1}\). Ammonium, NO\(_3^-\), and NO\(_2^-\) concentrations were low (<0.1 to 3 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\)) at most sites but sometimes higher (Table 1). Major exceptions were one Baffin Bay site in April 1999 with an NH\(_4^+\) concentration of 17 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\) and the Nueces River Mouth site in July 2001 with a NO\(_3^-\) concentration of 67 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\) (Table 1).

Nitrogen dynamics.—Measured nitrogen fluxes and transformation rates for the various systems are shown in Tables 2–5. Each value is a mean (in \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)) from replicate cores (\( n = 2–3 \)). Positive rates indicate net concentration increases, whereas negative values reflect removal from the water. Before \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) addition, NH\(_4^+\) flux ranged from \(-31\) to 231, with a mean of 60 \( \pm \) 10 (SE), versus ranges and means of \(-20\) to 32 and 3.2 \( \pm \) 1.3, for NO\(_3^-\), and \(-5.0\) to 10.6 and 1.7 \( \pm \) 0.5, for NO\(_2^-\). Net N\(_2\) flux ranged from \(-154\) (net N fixation) to 530 (net denitrification) with a mean of 19 \( \pm \) 16. Total N fixation, measured after \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) addition, ranged from 0 to 97 and had a mean of 32 \( \pm \) 6 versus a range of 4 to 70 and mean of 32 \( \pm \) 3 for total denitrification measured as N\(_2\). Note that these values do not include Laguna Madre Estuary results from April 1999 and August 1999, which had highest values for net denitrification, because \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) enrichment experiments were not done on cores from those sampling dates.

Interesting differences among stations were observed in how the \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) additions affected the fluxes of total NH\(_4^+\) and \(^{15}\)NH\(_4^+\) in the cores. In the Laguna Madre Estuary, mean NH\(_4^+\) flux increased to 262 \( \pm \) 81 for the samples analyzed after \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) addition versus 87 \( \pm \) 16 for the same samples before additions. Measured DNRA (i.e., \(^{15}\)NH\(_4^+\) accumulation from the added \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\)) ranged from 16 to 51 with a mean of 41 \( \pm \) 13 and accounted for only 23% of the mean difference (175) in NH\(_4^+\) flux before and after \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) addition in this region. Thus, the increase in total NH\(_4^+\) flux after \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) addition was about fourfold higher than accounted for by the measured DNRA for the same group of samples. By contrast, NH\(_4^+\) fluxes after \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) enrichment (27 \( \pm \) 20) were not distinguishable from those before addition (35 \( \pm \) 23) in Sabine Lake, where DNRA rates were low. Likewise, NO\(_3^-\) flux was not different before and after \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) addition in the lake. Mean fluxes overlapped with zero in both cases. Potential DNRA in Sabine Lake ranged from \(-1\) to 5.5, mean 0.9 \( \pm \) 0.8, versus a range and mean of \(-66\) to 68 and 16 \( \pm \) 16 for total denitrification (Table 3). In East Matagorda Bay, mean NH\(_4^+\) flux after \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) addition, 40 \( \pm \) 5, was higher than the mean value of 23 \( \pm \) 5 before the addition. Nitrogen fixation, 3 \( \pm \) 2, and \(^{15}\)NH\(_4^+\) accumulation from DNRA, 3.6 \( \pm \) 0.6, were low relative to denitrification, 22 \( \pm \) 4, after the addition (Table 4). Overall, N dynamics at these intermediate salinity stations were between values of Sabine Lake and the hypersaline Laguna Madre waters. In contrast to other sites, mean NO\(_2^-\) flux, an indicator of active N dynamics, was more than half of that for NO\(_3^-\) at East Matagorda Bay sites.

Results of the \(^{15}\)NH\(_4^+\) addition experiment conducted on East Matagorda Bay cores (Fig. 3) indicate that, although the initial net NH\(_4^+\) flux was positive, it represented steady-state equilibrium of exchange reactions between the water column and sediments. The addition of \(^{15}\)NH\(_4^+\) interrupted steady-state conditions and caused net flux of total NH\(_4^+\) to be \(-88\) the first day after addition, but it decreased to \(-15\) on the second day. Thus, total NH\(_4^+\) uptake (171 to 279) and release (83 to 216) rates, calculated after the \(^{15}\)NH\(_4^+\) isotope addition, were much greater than the measured net NH\(_4^+\) fluxes before or after the isotope addition. Note that the calculated total NH\(_4^+\) uptake and release demonstrate active exchange, but the measured net flux is more important ecologically because it represents the active flux of NH\(_4^+\) beyond steady-state sediment–water exchange.

The Nueces River Mouth site, sampled only in July 2001 at salinity 0.29, had a positive NH\(_4^+\) flux of about 40, but NO\(_3^-\) and NO\(_2^-\) fluxes were near zero (Table 5), even though NO\(_3^-\) concentration was high in the overlying water (Table 1). Net N fixation occurred at that station, and N fixation rates, after \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) enrichment, were more than twice as high as denitrification rates (Table 5). DNRA rates were low but measurable. The upper Corpus Christi Bay site, sampled only in July 2001 at salinity 2.0, had minimal N fluxes before \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) addition. Positive NH\(_4^+\) flux and measurable denitrification and DNRA rates, but no N fixation, were observed after the addition (Table 5).

Oxygen levels in overlying water were 0.98 ± 0.68 mg L<sup>−1</sup> in August and 5.3 ± 0.9 mg L<sup>−1</sup> in April (Table 1). Oxygen and sulfide transition zones were nearer to the sediment surface in August than in April (Fig. 4). Corresponding NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> fluxes were 86 ± 24 in August versus 2.9 ± 4.0 in April. Nitrate and NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> fluxes (respective means of 0.7 ± 1.4 and 0.5 ± 0.1) were much lower than NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> fluxes and did not show predictable patterns with season. Net N<sub>2</sub> flux indicated net denitrification in August (31 ± 4) but net N fixation in April (−65 ± 7). Total N-fixation rates were low in August (2.7 ± 2.7) but higher in April (30 ± 7). Denitrification rates were moderately, but not significantly, higher in August (52 ± 15) than in April (40 ± 5). DNRA rates were about six times higher in August (22 ± 6), when oxygen levels were low, than in April (3.6 ± 1.1) under norm-oxic conditions (Table 5). In contrast to results from other sites where DNRA was observed, significant increases in total NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> release after the <sup>15</sup>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> enrichment were not observed in August. Moderate increases in NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> release after enrichment were observed in April.

Discussion

Seasonal and regional rates of sediment N transformations along the Texas coast—Results from experiments in Texas coastal systems show that N transformations were dynamic at the sediment–water interface but varied spatially and temporally in relative importance and magnitude (Tables 2–5). The most active processes, in terms of net flux magnitude, were NH\(_4^+\) production from the sediments, N fixation, and denitrification. Reactions involving NO\(_3^-\) and NO\(_2^-\) may have been dynamic, but their concentrations and net changes remained low during most experiments, indicating that they were static or in steady-state equilibrium. Mean sediment NH\(_4^+\) fluxes before and after isotope additions were positive or near zero at all sites except Sabine Lake in December 2000, which showed net NH\(_4^+\) uptake. Observed NH\(_4^+\) accumulation and measurement of potential DNRA rates suggest that DNRA was a major component of total NH\(_4^+\) production at some stations.

Benthic nutrient fluxes in nine Gulf of Mexico estuaries have been examined by several investigators and reviewed (Twilley et al. 1999). In agreement with results from other Gulf of Mexico estuaries (Yoon and Benner 1992; Zimmerman and Benner 1994; Twilley et al. 1999), mean NH\(_4^+\) sediment regeneration rates (net fluxes) in the present study ranged from about 20 to 110 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\). Results for NO\(_3^-\) fluxes also follow patterns similar to previous results (Yoon and Benner 1992; Zimmerman and Benner 1994) in Texas estuaries, except for Guadalupe Estuary, which exhibited high NH\(_4^+\) uptake (\( \sim 150 \) \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)) and NO\(_3^-\) (plus

However, this observation may have been an exception to normal conditions as another study showed only moderate DIN fluxes in Guadalupe Estuary (Yoon and Benner 1992). Large spatial and temporal variations in N fluxes within and among estuaries make it difficult to discern patterns among them. For example, nutrient fluxes in Laguna Madre were lowest among estuaries examined in the earlier comparison (Twilley et al. 1999) but highest in the present comparison. The predominance of Texas brown tide in the 1990s may have affected this comparison. Dense populations of A. lagunensis remove NH₄⁺ from solution and keep concentrations low in the water (Gardner unpubl. data).

Sediment–atmosphere interactions: Is the sediment–water interface a site of net N₂ fixation (source) or net denitrification (sink) for available N?—Two approaches were taken to evaluate N fixation versus denitrification. First, net N₂ flux before \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) addition indicated whether atmospheric N₂ was a net source (N fixation) or sink (denitrification) of available N at the sediment–water interface. However, net changes do not reveal the extent to which N fixation and denitrification occur simultaneously. The isotope pairing approach (An et al. 2001) allows estimation of total rates for each process in the same cores but may not portray “actual rates” if the processes are affected by \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) addition.

In contrast to NH₄⁺ fluxes, which were almost always positive, net N₂ fluxes ranged from positive to negative values seasonally at the same sites and regionally among the sites. In Laguna Madre, net denitrification occurred on five occasions, net N fixation occurred twice, and zero net exchange occurred once. The opposite was observed in Sabine Lake, with N fixation dominating on six of seven occasions. In East Matagorda Bay, net N fixation was observed on 8 of 12 sampling occasions, but net rates were sometimes close to zero. Overall, net fixation was observed in the summer and winter (dry seasons) and net denitrification was observed in the spring and fall (wet seasons). Nitrogen fixation (Table 5) dominated in southeastern Corpus Christi Bay during April when O₂ levels were high in overlying waters (Fig. 4). However, denitrification dominated (Table 5) during summer when bottom water O₂ levels were low and the sulfide transition zone was near the sediment surface (Fig. 4). DNRA was six times higher at these sites in August than in April.

Denitrification rates from the present study were similar but, on average, higher than previous closed-chamber results in Texas estuaries (Yoon and Benner 1992; Zimmerman and Benner 1994). Underwater chamber results from Galveston Bay (An and Joye 2001) yielded higher denitrification rates than the present study and demonstrated that denitrification rates were higher in the light (mean N = 1000 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1} \)) than in the dark (mean N = 480 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1} \)).

Total N fixation versus denitrification rates, calculated in the enriched cores with the MIMS isotope pairing method, indicated that both processes proceeded simultaneously at comparable but different rates. For example, in Laguna Madre, mean postenrichment rates were 58 \( \pm \) 5 for N fixation, 32 \( \pm \) 5 for denitrification, and 41 \( \pm \) 13 for DNRA. Net N\(_2\) flux was 2.3 \( \pm \) 9.7 for the same cores before enrichment (excluding cores where enrichment experiments were not done). Unfortunately, \( ^{15} \)NO\(_3^-\) enrichments were not performed in April and August 1999 when highest net denitrification rates occurred. When these cores are included, net denitrification was dominant because of a large temporal effect. Results for both processes may be conservative since measurements did not account for N\(_2\)O production via incomplete denitrification. Also, both processes may be higher in natural light than dark or dim-light incubations because of labile organic matter production by photosynthesis (An and Joye 2001; An and Gardner 2002). Nitrogen fixation in Laguna Madre may have been underestimated since seagrasses were not included in experimental cores. Previous studies indicate that N fixation rates are high in seagrass beds where organic material is abundant (Paerl and Zehr 2000).

Data from the present study suggest that N fixation and denitrification are important and provide critical supply and removal mechanisms for available N in these productive systems. Although they occurred in both directions, net N\(_2\) fluxes across the sediment–water interface were comparable to NH\(_4^+\) fluxes and much higher than net NO\(_3^-\) or NO\(_2^-\) fluxes. This active exchange between atmospheric N\(_2\) and biotic N helps explain why Texas coastal systems have sufficient N

inputs to support high water-column N cycling rates, comparable to those in hypereutrophic ecosystems (Fig. 1), despite limited tributary nutrient inputs.

Relationship of DNRA to salinity and evidence for displacement of sediment-bound \( NH_4^+ \) by DNRA-produced \( NH_4^+ \)—Measuring N dynamics in sediment cores from a range of salinities provided an opportunity to examine relationships between N transformations and salinity and how they affect N removal or retention. Ammonium flux and DNRA rates increased with increasing salinity, but none of the other processes showed a significant salinity relationship. Denitrification: DNRA decreased significantly (\( p < 0.01 \)) with increasing salinity, suggesting that the fate of \( NO_3^- \) in surface sediments is related to salinity via DNRA and that DNRA is an important mechanism for retaining N in a biologically available form under saline conditions. DNRA also has been reported in other coastal systems (Koike and Hattori 1978; Sørensen 1978; Tobias et al. 2001). Enhancement of DNRA by sulfide- or sulfate-reducing bacteria (Rysgaard et al. 1996) is consistent (1) with the observed significant relationship between DNRA rates and salinity (with sulfate as a source) and (2) the large increase in DNRA rates observed when high sulfide concentrations, associated with low \( O_2 \), occurred near the sediment–water interface in Corpus Christi Bay (Fig. 4). The production of \( NH_4^+ \) by DNRA under conditions of high salinity may help explain why the Texas brown tide organism, A. lagunensis, which requires reduced N compounds as an N source, has thrived in the Laguna Madre Estuary when salinities were high (An and Gardner 2002). Aureoumbra lagunensis density in the estuary correlated directly with salinity at three stations sampled from July 1997 through October 1998 (Buskey et al. 2001).

Changes in total \( NH_4^+ \) release after \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) enrichment were proportional to but greater (\( r = 0.9998, a = -12.3, b = 7.41, p < 0.01 \)) than DNRA rates when mean rates from Laguna Madre, Sabine Lake, and East Matagorda Bay were compared. These results imply that \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) enrichment may affect total \( NH_4^+ \) production, presumably via DNRA. The slope of this relationship indicates that increased \( NH_4^+ \) release stimulated by \( NO_3^- \) enrichment was about seven times the \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) accumulation fraction on average. However, this relationship did not hold if Corpus Christi Bay data were included, particularly in August 2002 when higher DNRA rates appeared to relate to reducing conditions rather than salinity.

Observed differences between the increases in total \( NH_4^+ \) release after enrichment versus \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) accumulation at normoxic stations indicates that rates estimated from the latter measurement may have underestimated potential DNRA. The \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) produced from \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) via DNRA may have exchanged with sediment-bound \( ^{14}NH_4^+ \) (Rosenfeld 1979; Gardner et al. 1991; Seitzinger et al. 1991) as it diffused or migrated from the redox transition zone, where DNRA would occur, through the sediment to overlying water. If such exchange occurred, some \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) would have displaced \( ^{14}NH_4^+ \) on sediment exchange sites and resulted in increased \( ^{14}NH_4^+ \) release from the sediments. This exchange would cause the measurement of released \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) in the overflowing water to underestimate potential DNRA resulting from the \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) enrichment when there is a zone of oxygenated sediments above the redox transition zone. The active exchange of \( NH_4^+ \) between the water and sediments, observed in the \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) addition experiment on East Matagorda Bay cores (Fig. 3), illustrates why increases in total \( NH_4^+ \) release were greater than \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) accumulation after \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) addition.

The migration distance to the overlying water for \( NH_4^+ \) formed from DNRA would be minimized where the water is hypoxic and the redox transition zone is at or near the sediment surface (e.g., August 2002, Corpus Christi Bay). This temporal difference in redox transition depth is illustrated by comparing mean \( O_2 \) and sulfide profiles for Corpus Christi Bay stations sampled in August 2002 versus April 2003 (Fig. 4). The mean transition depth was \( \sim 1 \) mm in August versus 28 mm in April. In agreement with this concept, there was no evidence for \( ^{15}NH_4^+ : ^{14}NH_4^+ \) isotope exchange reactions in the core experiments from August 2002 (i.e., mean total \( NH_4^+ \) release showed a slight decrease despite the presence of measurable \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \); Table 5). However, mean total \( NH_4^+ \) release increased after \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) enrichment in April 2003 (Table 5) when \( O_2 \) and sulfide transition zones were deeper (Fig. 4).

Exchange reactions between free and bound \( NH_4^+ \) explain why measured \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) in outflow waters accounted for only a fraction of \( NO_3^- \) removal in isotope-addition experiments (An and Gardner 2002). A second possible sink for removed \( ^{15}NO_3^- \), which was not converted to \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \), is incomplete denitrification to \( N_2O \) and subsequent loss to the atmosphere (Smith et al. 1983). However, previous studies indicate that \( N_2O \) produced in estuarine sediments is small relative to \( N_2 \) (e.g., Seitzinger et al. 1983).

Evaluation of sediment–water N fluxes and transformations in Texas coastal systems offers insights about mechanisms controlling the sources and fate of available N in shallow, productive systems with variable and limited N inputs. Spatial and temporal similarities and differences in these processes among sites and seasons provides information about dominant cycling mechanisms and the importance of atmospheric \( N_2 \) as a source or sink for available N. The observed simultaneous N fixation and denitrification rates are consistent with the concept that available N compounds exchange actively with atmospheric \( N_2 \) and that N fixation is an important N source. Measurements of both processes were conservative since denitrification rates did not include \( N_2O \) production and assessments were not made under natural light or in the presence of seagrasses, conditions that would enhance production of labile organic compounds, which could serve as an energy source for N-transformation processes.

The observed relationship between sediment \( NH_4^+ \) release and salinity suggests that \( NH_4^+ \) regeneration increases with salinity. DNRA is an important process contributing to that trend. DNRA increased with salinity and was most important in Laguna Madre. DNRA also was important in southeastern Corpus Christi Bay during seasonal hypoxia. Comparison of potential DNRA rates estimated from \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) accumulation with those estimated from increased total \( NH_4^+ \) fluxes after \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) enrichment suggest that \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) accumulation can underestimate potential DNRA in sediments under oxygenated waters.

</page>

<page number="9">

Overall, our results are consistent with the concepts that N fixation is important in Texas estuaries and that DNRA helps retain available N in hypersaline estuaries. They help explain why N cycling rates in Laguna Madre and other Texas estuaries resemble those for hypereutrophic systems even though tributary inputs are limited.

Discussion Seasonal and regional rates of sediment N transformations along the Texas coast—Results from experiments in Texas coastal systems show that N transformations were dynamic at the sediment–water interface but varied spatially and temporally in relative importance and magnitude (Tables 2–5). The most active processes, in terms of net flux magnitude, were NH\(_4^+\) production from the sediments, N fixation, and denitrification. Reactions involving NO\(_3^-\) and NO\(_2^-\) may have been dynamic, but their concentrations and net changes remained low during most experiments, indicating that they were static or in steady-state equilibrium. Mean sediment NH\(_4^+\) fluxes before and after isotope additions were positive or near zero at all sites except Sabine Lake in December 2000, which showed net NH\(_4^+\) uptake. Observed NH\(_4^+\) accumulation and measurement of potential DNRA rates suggest that DNRA was a major component of total NH\(_4^+\) production at some stations. Benthic nutrient fluxes in nine Gulf of Mexico estuaries have been examined by several investigators and reviewed (Twilley et al. 1999). In agreement with results from other Gulf of Mexico estuaries (Yoon and Benner 1992; Zimmerman and Benner 1994; Twilley et al. 1999), mean NH\(_4^+\) sediment regeneration rates (net fluxes) in the present study ranged from about 20 to 110 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\). However, this observation may have been an exception to normal conditions as another study showed only moderate DIN fluxes in Guadalupe Estuary (Yoon and Benner 1992). Large spatial and temporal variations in N fluxes within and among estuaries make it difficult to discern patterns among them. For example, nutrient fluxes in Laguna Madre were lowest among estuaries examined in the earlier comparison (Twilley et al. 1999) but highest in the present comparison. The predominance of Texas brown tide in the 1990s may have affected this comparison. Dense populations of A. lagunensis remove NH₄⁺ from solution and keep concentrations low in the water (Gardner unpubl. data). Sediment–atmosphere interactions: Is the sediment–water interface a site of net N₂ fixation (source) or net denitrification (sink) for available N?—Two approaches were taken to evaluate N fixation versus denitrification. First, net N₂ flux before \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) addition indicated whether atmospheric N₂ was a net source (N fixation) or sink (denitrification) of available N at the sediment–water interface. However, net changes do not reveal the extent to which N fixation and denitrification occur simultaneously. The isotope pairing approach (An et al. 2001) allows estimation of total rates for each process in the same cores but may not portray “actual rates” if the processes are affected by \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) addition. In contrast to NH₄⁺ fluxes, which were almost always positive, net N₂ fluxes ranged from positive to negative values seasonally at the same sites and regionally among the sites. In Laguna Madre, net denitrification occurred on five occasions, net N fixation occurred twice, and zero net exchange occurred once. The opposite was observed in Sabine Lake, with N fixation dominating on six of seven occasions. In East Matagorda Bay, net N fixation was observed on 8 of 12 sampling occasions, but net rates were sometimes close to zero. Overall, net fixation was observed in the summer and winter (dry seasons) and net denitrification was observed in the spring and fall (wet seasons). Nitrogen fixation (Table 5) dominated in southeastern Corpus Christi Bay during April when O₂ levels were high in overlying waters (Fig. 4). However, denitrification dominated (Table 5) during summer when bottom water O₂ levels were low and the sulfide transition zone was near the sediment surface (Fig. 4). DNRA was six times higher at these sites in August than in April. Deposition, mineralization, and storage of carbon and nitrogen in sediments of the far northern and northern Great Barrier Reef shelf Daniel M. Alongi*, Lindsay A. Trott, John Pfitzner Australian Institute of Marine Science, PMB 3, Townsville MC, Qld. 4810, Australia Received 11 October 2006; received in revised form 10 July 2007; accepted 19 July 2007 Available online 1 August 2007 Abstract The flow of carbon and nitrogen in sediments of the far northern and northern sections of the Great Barrier Reef continental shelf was examined. Most of the organic carbon (81–94%) and total nitrogen (74–92%) depositing to the seabed was mineralized, with burial of carbon (6–19%) and nitrogen (8–20%) being proportionally less on this tropical shelf compared with other non-deltaic shelves. Differences in carbon and nitrogen mineralization among stations related best to water depth and proximity to river basins, with rates of mineralization based on net \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) production ranging from 17 to 39 (mean = 23) mmol C m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\). The overall ratio of O\(_2\):CO\(_2\) flux was 1.3, close to the Redfield ratio, implying that most organic matter mineralized was algal. Sulfate reduction was estimated to account for \( \approx 30\% \) (range: 6–62%), and denitrification for \( \approx 5\% \) (range: 2–13%), of total C mineralization; there was no measurable CH\(_4\) production. Discrepancies between \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) production across the sediment–water interface and sediment incubations suggest that as much as 5 mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (\( \approx 25\% \) of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) flux) was involved in carbonate mineral formation. Most microbial activity was in the upper 20 cm of sediment. Rates of net NH\(_4^+\) production ranged from 1.6 to 2.7 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\), with highly variable N\(_2\) fixation rates contributing little to total N input. Ammonification and nitrification rates were sufficient to support rapid rates of denitrification (range: 0.1–12.4 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)). On average, nearly 50% of total N input to the shelf sediment was denitrified. The average rates of sedimentation, mineralization, and burial of C and N were greater in the northern section of the shelf than in the far northern section, presumably due to higher rainfall and river discharge, as plankton production was similar between regions. The relative proportion of plankton primary production remineralized at the seafloor was in the range of 30–50% which is at the high end of the range found on other shelves. The highly reactive nature of these sediments is attributed to the deposition of high-quality organic material as well as to the shallowness of the shelf, warm temperatures year-round, and a variety of physical disturbances (cyclones, trawling) fostering physicochemical conditions favorable for maintaining rapid rates of microbial metabolism. The rapid and highly efficient recycling of nutrients on the inner and middle shelf may help to explain why the coral reefs on the outer shelf have remained unscathed from increased sediment delivery since European settlement. Introduction There is considerable concern about the impact and fate of terrestrially derived material entering the continental shelf of the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area (GBRWHA). Reduction in coral growth and a shift in the relative abundance and composition of corals and algae of nearshore fringing reefs, especially in inner shelf areas adjacent to intensively cultivated catchments, have been attributed to elevated availability of nutrients and suspended sediment loads (Fabricius et al., 2003). Intensification of land use and subsequent erosion of grazing land and crop land have resulted in an increase in sediment and nutrient delivery to the Great Barrier Reef (GBR) since the mid-1880s (Neil et al., 2002; Furnas, 2003). The magnitude of the increase is unclear, but more than one-half of sediment loading is estimated to come from grazing land, with 10% from crop land, and the remainder from natural erosion (Neil et al., 2002). Total sediment delivery is estimated at about 7 Mt y\(^{-1}\), with enhanced delivery possibly as high as 14–28 Mt y\(^{-1}\) (Neil et al., 2002; Furnas, 2003). The most intensive cultivation, and presumably the most intensive runoff, occurs in the latitudinal band of 16–18°S in the northern section of the GBRWHA. Less enhanced runoff occurs adjacent to less populated and cultivated catchments in the far northern section of the shelf. Nutrient cycling and inorganic and organic carbon dynamics is poorly understood on the GBR shelf, as most focus has been on cycling of elements on individual reefs rather than on non-reefal regions of the shelf. A number of studies have measured concentrations of dissolved inorganic nutrients along the length of the GBR, with data indicating concentrations typical of tropical waters under calm conditions, but elevated concentrations during periods of sustained winds when sediments are re-suspended, and during wet season plumes. GBR waters are characterized by N:P ratios of particulate matter of 8:1 and dissolved N:P ratios of 14:1 (Furnas, 2003). These low ratios likely reflect P adsorption onto inorganic particles, but may possibly indicate material of good nutritive value (Furnas et al., 1995). Sedimentation fluxes (based on data from sediment traps; Furnas et al., 1995) have been difficult to obtain in such shallow waters as most material recovered appears to be re-suspended matter, mucus, and other colloidal material. Stoichiometric ratios vary widely, but suggest fairly labile material settling to the seabed. Nutrient cycling in non-reefal GBR sediments is not well characterized, although several studies have pointed to \( \mu \)M concentrations of dissolved inorganic nutrients in interstitial water and rapid microbial activity (Alongi, 1989; Lourey et al., 2001). High rates of benthic microbial activity and lack of vertical profiles of dissolved and particulate nutrient concentrations suggest little burial of reactive organic matter, in agreement with low burial rates measured in the central GBR (Brunskill et al., 2002). The physical and biological complexity of the GBR limits the application of results from one section of the shelf to another. The GBR province is the exemplar of a carbonate rimmed shelf, and is one of the world’s largest continental margins with extensive mixed terrigenous–carbonate sedimentary facies (Hopley et al., 2007). The GBR shelf is a passive continental margin with a low seafloor gradient of <1:1000. The development and tectonic setting of this shelf is well understood compared with other tropical continental shelves. The shelf is wide (30–150 km) and shallow (<80 m at shelf break), encompassing an area of 225,000 km\(^2\), and is uniquely rimmed on the outer shelf margin by nearly 2500 individual coral reefs comprising the GBR, which stretches over 2000 km (10–24°S) parallel to the Queensland coast (Maxwell, 1968). The GBR shelf shares some characteristics with other tropical shelves, such as (1) a benthic fauna dominated by large epibenthos (e.g., echinoderms), lancelets, and large Foraminifera; (2) infaunal communities composed mostly of pioneering, small opportunists that surface deposit—and/or suspension feed; (3) abundant demersal assemblages, especially crustaceans; (4) intermittent intrusions of upwelled, nutrient-rich water; and (5) a summer wet season in which cyclones and monsoonal rains occur. The shallowness of the shelf in concert with severe summer weather, extensive trawling, and erratic nutrient inputs fosters plankton and benthic communities adapted to respond quickly to such disturbances and fluctuating rates of food supply. A sharp, across-shelf gradient of sedimentary facies from inshore terrigenous mud and quartz sand to mixed terrigenous–carbonate deposits mid-shelf to impure and pure carbonate within and between reefs on the outer margin is the dominant geological characteristic of the shelf (Hopley et al., 2007). In the far northern (Fig. 1a) and northern (Fig. 1b) sectors, this gradient narrows but persists from the south. On the inner shelf, the seaward limit Fig. 1. Maps of the location of benthic stations in the (a) far northern and (b) northern sections of the Great Barrier Reef shelf. Depth contours are in meters. of the coastal zone is dynamic, varying in time and space and formed when turbid inshore and estuarine waters mix and are trapped along the coast; the coastal boundary breaks down under strong winds and river discharge (Wolanski and Ridd, 1990). River floods typically last for a few days and enter the shelf as plumes mostly in summer; runoff is negligible the rest of the year. Coastal boundary zones often form in bays sheltered by capes and headlands. Coastal waters move slowly longshore towards the headlands but may be periodically diverted as an ebb tidal jet peeling off from the headland, presumably enriching the middle shelf. Neither eddies formed by the rugged coastline nor longshore currents formed by the southeast trades can propagate in sheltered waters due to friction. Within the coastal boundary layer, dispersion of nutrients and particulate matter is by tidal diffusion only, especially when winds are light. It is for this reason that there is constant exchange between estuaries and the coastal boundary layer, but much slower rates of mixing between inshore and offshore waters (Wolanski, 1994). The phenomenon of trapping due to friction and the presence of coastal boundary zones ensure that most terrigenous sediment persists as a narrow band along the inner shelf. The regional distribution of Holocene terrigenous deposits and the sharp across-shelf gradient from terrigenous to carbonate facies have been well described (Maxwell, 1968; Belperio and Searle, 1988; Larcombe and Carter, 2004; Hopley et al., 2007). Evidence from X-radiographs and radionuclide profiles shows that episodes of re-suspension, re-deposition, and intense reworking of surface deposits are common on the inner shelf (Alongi and Christoffersen, 1992; Brunskill et al., 2002). The sediment-starved middle shelf is a zone of transitional (30–60% carbonate) and impure (60–80% CaCO₃) carbonate facies. Surface water speeds commonly reach 50 cm s⁻¹ or more, but do not cause significant bedload transport. A recent analysis (Larcombe and Carter, 2004) has argued that cyclones transport post-storm mud drapes on top of the sandy middle shelf bed that are fully remixed into the sand facies by persistent bioturbation. Along shelf, cyclone-driven flow produces shelf-parallel, bed-sediment transport that is delimited as dunes, ribbons, or small dune areas on the middle shelf. Such strong flows (up to 130–200 cm s\(^{-1}\)) have resulted in erosion of Pleistocene deposits that are often exposed beneath a veneer of muddy sand and unconsolidated shell. This veneer, the net sedimentation of \( \approx 10,000 \) y of seabed exposure, is continually eroded and re-suspended by cyclones; mud in suspension is transported northwards along shelf and advected landwards. The result is dunes and ribbons of bioclastic deposits up to \( \approx 15 \) cm thick on the middle shelf (Belperio and Searle, 1988; Larcombe and Carter, 2004). It is on this portion of the shelf that epibenthic communities are most abundant and diverse, dominated by echinoderms, bryozoans, large ascidians, sponges, and Foraminifera (Alongi, 1989). In this paper, we detail studies of benthic metabolic rates and pathways of carbon and nitrogen cycling at inner and middle shelf sites proximal to impacted catchments on the northern GBR and to less heavily impacted catchments on the far northern GBR shelf. Some first-order calculations are also made to understand the benthic contribution to nutrient dynamics on these sections of the shelf and how (or if) they differ to earlier studies in the central section of the GBR shelf. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study sites On the far northern shelf, three stations (Stas. HAY, HAN, and BUK) were chosen based on their proximity to coastal reefs. Stas. HAY, HAN, and BUK were, respectively, located within 1.5 km northwest of the leeward side of Hay, Hannah, and Burkett Islands, a series of low wooded islands with diverse fringing reefs (Table 1). These islands compose the Claremont Isles Group on the middle shelf, and are surrounded by a seabed composed of mostly transitional carbonate sand (Maxwell, 1968; Hopley, 2004). A fourth station (Sta. PCB) was situated 7 km off the Normanby River in Princess Charlotte Bay (Fig. 1a) The Normanby River is the largest drainage system on the far northern shelf. Sta. FIZ was sited within seagrass beds 1.5 km off the windward southern side of Fitzroy Island, and Sta. HIG was located within 7.5 km northeast off the mouth of the Mulgrave–Russell Rivers and 1 km off the northwestern leeward side of High Island, one of the islands of the Frankland Islands Group. Also, within this island group was Sta. RUS, located within seagrass beds between Russell Island, Round Island, and Normandy Island. Sta. FIZ was visited only once in July 2000, but the other stations were sampled in July 2000 (winter), February 2001 (summer), September 2001, September 2002 (dry spring), and February 2003 (summer). On the first two cruises, sediment cores to a maximum penetration depth of 20 cm were taken using a modified 0.027 m\(^2\) Bouma boxcorer. On the last three cruises, boxcorer samples were taken for flux measurements across the sediment–water interface (see below), and 1-m length cores were taken using a Kasten corer and were handled as described in Brunskill et al. (2002). 2.2. Sediment granulometry and solid-phase elements Boxcorer and Kasten corer samples were used for analysis of sediment grain size and percent sand, silt, and clay using the standardized procedure of Folk (1974) on an automated particle size counter. Sediments were classified as mud, sand, sandy mud, or muddy sand, based on the definitions in Folk (1974). Further sub-samples from the boxcores were taken at 2-cm intervals to a depth of 20 cm on the first two cruises and at 15–20 irregularly spaced intervals to a depth of 1 m on the last three cruises. These sub-samples were frozen at sea, then thawed and wet and dry weighted to determine water content, and ground to a fine powder for determination of total carbon and total nitrogen on a Perkin-Elmer 2400 CHNS/O Series II analyzer and for total organic carbon on a Shimadzu TOC analyzer with solid sampler. Other elements (P, S, Mn, Fe) were determined after strong acid digestion on a Varian Liberty inductively coupled atomic emission spectrometer following the procedure of Loring and Rantala (1992). Total inorganic carbon was assumed as CaCO₃, and was determined by difference between the total carbon and total organic carbon concentrations. 2.3. Mass sediment accumulation Mass sediment accumulation rates (MAR) were determined from gamma spectrometric measurements of \(^{210}\mathrm{Pb}\), \(^{137}\mathrm{Cs}\), and other radionuclides made on sequentially sliced duplicate 100-cm-long cores taken using the Kasten corer (Brunskill et al., 2002). Each core was cut into 2-cm slices from the sediment surface to 20-cm depth, then into 4-cm slices to the bottom of the core. Gamma ray measurements were made on 50–150 g dried and ground sediment from each slice packed by a 10 metric ton hydraulic press into a custom designed gas-tight plastic container. Four Canberra GL2020R/S special low-energy, low-background planar germanium detectors housed inside 10-cm thick, lead-walled castles with steel liners were used to collect the gamma photons. Energy spectra were calibrated with standards consisting of known low-activity spikes of suitable nuclides from Amersham and CANMET calibrated sources in silica sand and sand/calcium carbonate matrices. Minimum detection limits, in Bq kg⁻¹ dry weight of sediment, for a 50 g sample counted for 1 d are 4 for \(^{210}\mathrm{Pb}\), 0.5 for \(^{226}\mathrm{Ra}\), 1.0 for \(^{228}\mathrm{Ra}\), 0.5 for \(^{228}\mathrm{Th}\), 1.5 for \(^{234}\mathrm{Th}\), and 0.7 for \(^{137}\mathrm{Cs}\). Interpretations of the radiochemical profiles were done with several sub-models incorporating weighted least-squares regression analysis (Robbins, 1978, 1979). Sediment mass accumulation rates (MAR) were multiplied by average TOC and TN sediment concentrations in the same cores to provide estimates of accumulation of these elements. 2.4. Solute fluxes Solute fluxes across the sediment–water interface were measured using three sets of three closed opaque chambers (volume: 1 l; area: 82 cm²) from which \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \), O₂, and dissolved inorganic nutrient and metal samples were taken at 3 h intervals for 12–18 h. Two chambers were gently placed into each of three boxcorer samples (\( n = 9 \); total area = 738 cm²), which were incubated in the dark in a running seawater bath to maintain ambient seawater temperature. Each chamber had a propeller-electric motor unit and two sampling ports on opposite sides of the chamber (Alongi et al., 2006). Small replicate chambers were used to determine the extent of small-scale variability between replicate boxcores and to ensure adherence to the assumptions for analysis of variance (Sokal and Rohlf, 1995). Dissolved oxygen was measured using an O₂ probe (TPS™ Model WP-82 DO meters) placed into one sampling port; the other port was fitted with plastic tubing to draw off 10 ml samples for \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) and dissolved nutrients and metals. The samples for \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) and dissolved inorganic nutrients were filtered (0.45 μm Minisart® filters) and either kept cool and dark (\( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \)) or frozen until analysis. Concentrations of NH₄⁺, NO₂⁻ + NO₃⁻, and PO₄³⁻ were determined using automated techniques (Ryle et al., 1981; Ryle and Wellington, 1982). Concentrations of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) were determined using the procedure of Hall and Aller (1992). Dissolved metals were analyzed as detailed in Section 2.6. 2.5. Sulfate reduction Rates of sulfate reduction were measured in triplicate 2.7-cm diameter plastic cores taken to a depth of 20 cm from boxcores on the first three cruises. Cores were injected at 2-cm intervals with carrier-free \(^{35}\mathrm{SO}_4\) (Fossing and Jorgensen, 1989), incubated for 6–9 h, and then terminated by fixing sediments in 20% zinc acetate. On the last two cruises, triplicate 2.7-cm plastic cores were taken horizontally from Kasten cores at 0–2 cm and at various intervals to 1 m. The samples were capped at both ends and the middle 2 cm of each sample was injected and processed as described above. Samples were then frozen until a two-step distillation procedure was used to determine the fraction of reduced radiolabel shunted into the acid-volatile sulfide (AVS) and chromium-reducible sulfur (CRS) pools. 2.6. Net metal, \( \sum CO_2 \), and \( NH_4^+ \) production Rates of net production of dissolved metals, \( \sum CO_2 \), and \( NH_4^+ \) from sediments at each site were measured by incubating two sets of duplicate sediment cores taken from boxcores on the first three cruises, and from sub-samples taken from Kasten cores on the last two cruises (Alongi et al., 2006). From the boxcores, one entire set of 20-cm length cores were incubated, mixed, and placed in large opaque glass bottles for 6 d in a N_2-filled glove bag, to give integrated rates over the top 20 cm. The other set of cores was sliced immediately at 4-cm intervals and each sediment cake was placed into separate plastic cassettes containing a 0.4 \( \mu \)m Poretics\textregistered{} filter and squeezed on a pore water extractor under gentle N_2 pressure. Each sample was first squeezed for \( \sum CO_2 \) and metals, then each sample was mixed in 1 M KCl solution and after 2–3 h squeezed again to obtain total extractable \( NH_4^+ \). The whole cores incubated for 6 d were processed by taking sub-samples and upscaling reaction rates to the entire sediment volume. From the Kasten cores, separate sets of samples were taken at various depth intervals, incubated in sealed opaque glass jars at in situ temperature in a water bath for 6–10 d, and processed as described above. Samples were processed for \( \sum CO_2 \) and dissolved inorganic nutrients as described earlier, and pore water Cl\(^-\), S, Fe, Ca, Mg, Sr, and Mn were analyzed on the Varian ICP-MS. pH was measured from the Kasten cores using a Model PBFC pH electrode which was allowed to equilibrate for 10–15 min before readings were taken on a TPS LC 80 meter. The pH electrode was calibrated using 6.00, 7.00, and 8.00 NIST standards. Saturation states for calcite and aragonite were calculated using the formula, \( \Omega_{CALITE, ARAGONITE} = [Ca^{2+}][CO_3^{2-}]/K_{CALCITE, ARAGONITE} \), in which the apparent solubility products for calcite (\( K_{CALCITE} \)) and aragonite (\( K_{ARAGONITE} \)) fit to temperature and salinity by Mucci (1983) were used (Millero, 1995). The carbonate concentration was calculated from the pH and \( \sum CO_2 \) data in estimating the second apparent dissociation constant of carbonic acid at the appropriate temperature and salinity (Mehrbach et al., 1973; Millero, 1995). 2.7. Nitrification, denitrification, and nitrogen fixation Nitrification was estimated using the acetylene inhibition technique (Sloth et al., 1992). Six opaque chambers were inserted into boxcorer samples as for the other solute flux measurements and incubated identically, except that three chambers immediately received 50 ml of acetylene-saturated seawater to inhibit nitrification. Sediment–water fluxes of NH_4\(^+\) were measured in both sets of chambers. The difference in the slope of NH_4\(^+\) vs. time between the treatments was assumed to correspond to the rate of nitrification. Denitrification was measured from replicate sediment samples taken from boxcores using the N_2-gas flux technique (Nowicki, 1994). Fluxes of CH_4 were measured in the same chambers. Open-ended bottles were carefully pushed 8–10 cm into the sediment (volume: 230–385 cm\(^3\)) and samples were kept at ambient temperature in an aerated running seawater bath until return to the laboratory. Any obvious surface fauna was removed with tweezers before each sample was extruded into a gas-tight glass chamber (height = 23.5 cm; i.d. = 7.6 cm). Sediments in each chamber were covered with seawater sparged with either 80%He/20%O_2 mixture (four experimental chambers per site) or 100% He (one to two control chambers per site) to remove N_2 and, in the case of the experimental cores, to maintain dissolved O_2 concentrations. The overlying water in each sealed chamber was stirred continuously. All chambers were incubated for 9 d in the dark at ambient temperatures. In the experimental chambers, the gas phase was flushed every 8 h for the first 2 d with a 80% He/20% O_2 mixture, and again the water overlying the sediment was periodically replaced with low-N_2 seawater after 3 d. The control chambers were treated similarly but incubated under anoxic conditions to block nitrification and denitrification. A 100% He-flushed, low-N_2 seawater exchange was carried out after 3 d, wherein all control and experimental chambers were sealed and gas samples were withdrawn for measurement of gas concentrations in the headspace. The accumulation of N_2 and O_2 in the headspace was measured each day for the next 5 d using an MTI Analytical Instruments P200 gas chromatograph. Calibration standards were run with each set of samples using a certified gas mixture. Background de-gassing of N_2 from the control chambers was subtracted from the total N_2 flux measured in the experimental chambers to derive the rate of N_2 flux due to denitrification (Nowicki, 1994). Denitrification rates were calculated as the average rate of triplicate cores from each site, from 3 to 4 individual incubation periods. CH_4 accumulation rates in the gas headspaces were considered de novo synthesis and were calculated as the average rate of triplicate cores from each site using oxic chambers only. Nitrogen fixation in sediments at each site was measured in three to four dark and clear chambers using the acetylene reduction technique (Capone, 1993). Samples were taken by inserting open-ended chambers (surface area: 64 cm^2) into the sediment to a depth of 5 cm. The chambers and soil plugs were then gently withdrawn with minimal disturbance. The bases of the chambers were sealed with PVC caps containing an inert rubber plate. A 10% acetylene/air mixture was created (sediment volume: 320 cm^3), added in the water phase, and the headspace was sampled immediately and at 3 h intervals, with a final sampling at \( \approx 20 \) h. Acetylene and ethylene were analyzed simultaneously by gas chromatography. The ethylene rates were converted to rates of N_2 fixation using the theoretical factor of 4 C_2H_2 molecules equalling 1 N molecule (Capone, 1993). 3. Results 3.1. Pore water chemistry Vertical profiles of SO\(_4^{2-}\) and Cl\(^-\) showed no significant change with increasing sediment depth, with SO\(_4^{2-}\) concentrations equivalent to the overlying water; no free sulfide was detected (data not shown). In contrast, total dissolved Fe concentrations were usually below detection limits (Fe = 0.18 \( \mu \)M; Mn = 0.04 \( \mu \)M). Vertical profiles of NH\(_4^+\) showed increasing concentrations with sediment depth although values were highly variable between replicate cores and depths; PO\(_4^{3-}\) and Mn concentrations did not vary significantly with sediment depth (data not shown). The ratios of pore water Ca, Mg, and Sr with respect to Cl suggested supersaturation compared with the overlying water-column values. These results are supported by the saturation states for calcite and aragonite (Fig. 4). 3.4. Solute fluxes across the sediment–water interface Rates of \( \sum \)CO\(_2\) flux from surface sediments varied significantly between stations and seasons (Fig. 5, top) with no clear seasonal or site differences owing to significant site \( \times \) season interactions (two-way ANOVA). Rates of O\(_2\) flux showed similar patterns (Fig. 5, middle) with no clear differences among treatments. Ratios of O\(_2\):\( \sum \)CO\(_2\) flux (Fig. 5, bottom) ranged between 0.7 and 3.5. There was good agreement between both measurements (Fig. 6) with a significant (\( P < 0.001 \)) regression coefficient of 1.3. Flux rates of dissolved NH\(_4\), PO\(_4^{3-}\), and Si(OH)\(_4^+\) were in most instances out of the sediment (Fig. 7). NO\(_3^-\) fluxes were always into the sediment (Fig. 7). Fluxes of Fe, Mn, Ca, Mg, and Sr were not significant at any of the stations. Fig. 4. Vertical plots of the calculated saturation states of calcite and aragonite at eight stations. 3.5. Metal, \( \sum CO_2 \), and \( NH_4^+ \) production Incubation of sediment from discrete intervals resulted in the net production of \( \sum CO_2 \) and \( NH_4^+ \) (Figs. 8 and 9), but no net production of Fe or Mn. Vertical profiles from September 2002 and February 2003 showed a decline of net \( \sum CO_2 \) and \( NH_4^+ \) production with increasing sediment depth (Figs. 8 and 9), but with some measurable production to a depth of 1 m at Stas. HAY, BUK, CNS, and HIG. For most stations, the bulk of C and N mineralization occurred in the upper 20 cm or less. Depth-integrated rates of C and N mineralization ranged from 9.2 to 40.2 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) and 630 to 4450 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 5) with no consistent seasonal or site differences, as site differences varied between seasons and seasonal differences varied by location (Table 5). The ratio of C:N mineralization ranged from 5.8 to 33.5 with a overall mean of 12.6. Rates of N mineralization correlated inversely (\( r = -0.768; P < 0.01 \)) with water depth. 3.6. Sulfate reduction Sulfate-reducing activity was detected to a sediment depth of 1 m, but there was an overall decline with increasing sediment depth at all sites (Fig. 10). Rates of sulfate reduction were not significantly different between stations during most seasons (\( P > 0.05 \)) with depth-integrated rates ranging from 0.6 to 13.1 mmol S m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 5). Most \( ^{35}S \) radiotracer was recovered in the CRS fraction (Table 5). Rates of sulfate reduction correlated inversely with the C:S ratio in the sediments (\( r = -0.66; P < 0.05 \)). 3.7. Nitrogen processes and \( CH_4 \) production \( CH_4 \) was not detected in any of the sediment incubations. Denitrification ranged from 110 to 12,408 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 6) but was highly variable within stations and seasons. There were site differences but these were inconsistent with season. There was sufficient nitrification to support denitrification, with nitrification rates (Table 6) ranging from 500 to 2970 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) with no consistent differences between stations and seasons. On 12 of 23 occasions when nitrogen fixation was measurable, rates were low and variable, ranging from 10 to 374 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 6). 3.8. Organic carbon and total nitrogen budgets Measurement of the major individual transformation processes allowed us to construct organic carbon and nitrogen budgets for all nine stations. A budget for organic carbon (Table 7), using seasonally averaged figures, showed that 81–94% of organic carbon that deposited on the shelf was mineralized over the upper 1 m, especially within the upper 20 cm, with little (6–19%) carbon burial. Sulfate reduction was estimated to account for \( \approx 30\% \) (range: 6–62%), and denitrification for \( \approx 5\% \) (range: 2–13%), of total C mineralization. There was a significant positive relationship between sedimentation rate and the percentage of carbon preserved (Fig. 11, top), but the relationship between mineralization and sedimentation rate was not significant (Fig. 11, bottom). Total C input correlated inversely with water depth (\( r = -0.57; P < 0.10 \)). On the average, the C:N of mineralization ranged from <10 at Stas. Our data indicate that the patterns of organic carbon mineralization relate best to distance from the coast (expressed as water depth in the statistical analyses) and proximity to river basins, rather than simple geography. There were no clear differences in rates of planktonic primary production between the far northern and northern sectors of the shelf (M. Furnas, pers. comm.). The high mineralization efficiencies (81–94%; average: 89%) translate into low burial efficiencies (6–19%; average \( \approx 11\%\)). It is likely that the true burial rates are lower. The radiochemical profiles resulted in model estimates of sedimentation ranging from 1.4 to 5.8 kg m\(^{-2}\) y\(^{-1}\) and our results agree well with earlier data from Princess Charlotte Bay and off Cairns (Torgersen et al., 1983; Brady et al., 1994). However, storms and other physical disturbances, such as trawling, result in a fining upwards of sediment. Experiments with GBR sediments mimicking these disturbances found that the net result of an increase in the proportion of fine particles toward the sediment–water interface may incorrectly suggest recent increases in sedimentation (Towler and Smith, 2000). Some of our radionuclide profiles (e.g., Sta. HIG) showed some evidence of episodes of large slabs of sediment depositing, as well as scouring of seabed. The burial rates reported here must be considered as maximal rates. The most likely explanation for these low burial rates is the fact that the GBR shelf is shallow, warm year-round, and therefore subject to intense disturbance of the sediment surface and sediment mixing by cyclones, storms, and trawling. This idea is supported by the vertical distribution of benthic infauna and X-radiographic evidence of sediments further south near Hinchinbrook Island (Alongi and Christoffersen, 1992). Most infauna are small sized, of low abundance, and living predominantly in the upper 2–5 cm, but large, deep-dwelling equilibrium species are rare. X-radiographs consistently show that the sedimentary fabric consists of shell-gravel bands and cross-bedding features attributable to episodes of erosion. Much of the inner and middle shelf is above the mean shoaling depth for wind waves and tidal scouring. When spring tides (up to 3.8 m) coincide with low intervals of sea level (which oscillates in this region up to 35 cm), cycles of erosion, re-suspension, and deposition occur. Such events can occur several times a year as they may not be solely dependent on astronomical tides (Wolanski and Ridd, 1990; Wolanski, 1994). As most carbon remineralization occurs in the upper sediment layers, most decomposition is likely to have been accomplished by aerobic bacteria as many of the attributes of these sites, including fully oxic conditions in the bottom water, rapid water currents, a significant sand fraction, and high rates of surface sediment disturbance, may promote extensive aerobic respiration. The exceptions to this caveat are Stas. PCB and CNS, which were composed of fine-grained terrigenous silt and clay particles having the highest Fe and Mn concentrations. The \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) uptake rates were high (range: 12–63 mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\); average \( \approx 25 \)) compared to other shelves (Canfield, 1993; Henrichs, 1993; Aller et al., 1996; Canfield et al., 2005; Emerson and Hedges, 2006) but very similar to rates measured further north in the Gulf of Papua (average \( \approx 23 \) mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\); Aller et al., 2004). Aerobic respiration cannot be readily separated from possible manganese and iron reduction, but several pieces of evidence imply that metal reduction may be a minor proportion of total carbon oxidation at these sites. First, large relative contributions from metal reducers are ordinarily found in fine-grained terrigenous deposits, where high content of diagenetically active iron and manganese oxides, well-oxygenated bottom water, and a moderately high input of reactive organic matter support a large bioturbating infauna (Canfield et al., 2005). In the GBR, total solid-phase Fe and Mn concentrations and reactivity are low (Alongi et al., 1993), and although inputs of reactive organic matter are high, the infauna, as discussed above, are small sized and live primarily within the upper 2–5 cm; there are rarely any infaunal organisms that build deep tubes or burrows. Physical disturbances are common, but mostly restricted to the upper sediment deposits. X-radiographs from most of our sites rarely indicated any significant biogenic structures beneath the surface layers. So, continuous reworking by infauna is unlikely to be a significant mechanism to replenish the supply of metal oxides to support metal reduction. Second, although some oxidation likely occurred upon sample handling, some nitrate was found in the pore water beneath the sediment surface; measurable Fe reduction normally does not occur within zones of significant NO\(_3^-\) concentrations (Walter and Burton, 1990). Third, evidence from other studies suggests that Mn reduction is insignificant except at sites with unusually high Mn oxide concentrations, and in certain intertidal habitats where plant roots and bioturbating fauna can reoxidize Mn (and Fe) oxides (Canfield et al., 2005, Table 5.8). Finally, we did not measure any net production of dissolved Mn or Fe either in surface sediment incubations or across the sediment–water interface. Excluding Stas. PCB and CNS, all of the other stations were either sandy or calcareous or both, implying insufficient reactive metal oxides necessary for Fe or Mn reduction. In adjacent sites on Sudbury and Arlington Reefs (Alongi et al., 2006), no evidence of Fe or Mn reduction was found, in agreement with earlier studies that have indicated unsuitable conditions for metal reduction in carbonate-rich, metal-poor deposits (Walter et al., 1993). The potentially significant role of aerobic respiration in these sediments is in agreement with measurements made in other carbonate-dominated sediments (Boucher et al., 1994; Werner et al., 2006). Episodes of re-suspension and deposition may foster aerobic pathways by recharging the dissolved oxygen supply in surface sediments. The differences between the diffusive fluxes (average = 16.6 mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)) and production fluxes (average = 21.6 mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)) of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) indicate either that a moderate amount (\( \approx 5 \) mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)) of remineralized \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) is involved in authigenic mineral formation or that transport-reaction processes are not in steady state. Most of the imbalances in \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) flux were <10% of total C remineralization, well within the systematic error of many of the multiple methods used. No net fluxes of Ca, Fe, or Mn were measured across the sediment–water interface at any of the stations. The rates of DIC generated in the subsurface sediment incubations are not in balance with the amounts of Ca, Mg, and Sr calculated to precipitate in the deeper sediments, but the relationship between sulfate reduction and carbonate mineral kinetics is complex and non-linear, with aragonite supersaturation occurring at both low and high rates of sulfate reduction (Walter and Burton, 1990), and such may be the case in the GBR deposits. The rates of sulfate reduction were similar to those measured in other regions of the GBR shelf (Alongi, 1992; Alongi et al., 2006), and accounted for 6–62% of total carbon mineralization. Most radiolabel was shunted into the CRS fraction and although sulfate reduction was measurable to 1 m at some locations, most activity was confined to surficial sediments. The diminished role of sulfate reduction at some locations is consistent with low S content of sediment and C:S ratios (range: 2.7–5.5) generally higher than in normal marine shelf sediments (Canfield et al., 2005). Although not as dramatic, this pattern is similar to that found in tropical deltaic sediments off the Amazon and Fly Rivers (Aller et al., 1996, 2004). In this study, C:S ratios correlated with rates of sulfate reduction, and the lack of sulfides detected in the pore water suggests that there is comparatively little preservation of S (or Fe) as stable sulfide minerals. Total carbon oxidation rates did not correlate with sedimentation rate. The lack of a significant correlation suggests that other factors such as mixing/physical disturbance and the narrow seasonal range of water temperature play an important role in influencing rates of total carbon oxidation. Empirical and modelling studies have shown that re-suspension of surface sediments stimulates mineralization by aerating sediments, mixing labile organic matter, and by stimulating bacterial growth and minimizing preservation of carbon (Wainwright and Hopkinson, 1997; Aller and Aller, 2004). In a shallow water column, a tight coupling is likely between benthic and pelagic mineralization and nutrient turnover (Alongi and McKinnon, 2005). This scenario is similar to that suggested by Aller (1998, 2004) for mobile shelf muds which appear to act as suboxic, fluidized bed reactors. Comparison of benthic carbon oxidation with pelagic primary production (M. Furnas, pers. comm.) indicates that the relative proportion of water-column organic carbon production remineralized in GBR sediments is in the range of 30–50% which is slightly higher than the range found in other shelf environments (Gattuso et al., 1998). Benthic microalgal production also contributes to benthic remineralization, as seagrass beds were found, but primary production was not measured, at several stations. Terrestrial C input also contributes to benthic carbon oxidation. Using floating sediment traps, Furnas (per. comm.) measured rates of organic carbon sedimentation greater than 3 × benthic mineralization rates. Most of this material was re-suspended sediment, but nearly a third was flocculent or colloidal aggregates, perhaps formed as a result of microbial mediation and exudation of extracellular by-products, as described by Fabricius et al. (2003) in the GBR.
